utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Could the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable, Mr. Puhalac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good morning to you, Mr. Puhalac. Did you hear me, Mr. Puhalac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought you were just making a pause, and I would appreciate if you actually do that, and that we speak slowly so that everything makes it into the transcript. Mr. Puhalac, did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see in e-court 1D7898. 1D7898.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you now see that statement before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to read and sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see the last page so that the witness may verify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please do not let this paragraph 19 confuse you. The Trial Chamber found that it wasn't really necessary for these proceedings, but everything else remains unchanged. Does this statement reflect truthfully what you've said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you that were put to you when the statement was taken, would your answers in essence be the same?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this statement, and I will have an additional document, but I do not have any associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just see -- I think it's a translation error in paragraph 2 in the English version, third line from the bottom. The word used is "Lukavac," whereas I think it should be "Lukavica," if I'm not mistaken. And I'm actually not sure in the same paragraph if the witness meant to say "Sokoc" or "Sokolac," but the Lukavac reference is certainly a translation error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you can clarify with the witness, Mr. Karadzic. Otherwise, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3104, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read the summary statement of Mr. Puhalac, Tomislav, and then we'll clarify things live. Now I will read it in English. [In English] Tomislav Puhalac was member of the BH State Security Service from 1977 to April 1992. He later worked at the National Security Agency in Sokolac. In August 1992, he was appointed deputy chief of the Centre of National Security in Lukavica, Sarajevo. When the national parties in BH won the elections and the SDA and HDZ coalition was formed, pressure began to be exerted on the Serbian people in general, affecting Serb employees of the RSUP. Means Ministry of Interior of Republic of BH. When Alija Izetbegovic -- Alija Delimustafic became the head of the MUP, the appointment of the Serb employees was limited and actions were taken to prevent their participation in the decision-making process and other important and sensitive issues. Extremists were appointed into the higher positions within the police and state security department. Information had been obtained that Muslim forces were establishing paramilitary and parastate organisations. These organisations were obtaining weapons via Croatia and Islamic countries, and although confiscations were made and recorded, the undertaking of further legal measures was hindered. During 1991, reserve police forces were mobilised by Alija Delimustafic. However, only new forces loyal to the SDA were used. Serb members of the police force began to abandon their jobs or move and therefore a number of police stations and reserve forces became fully mono-ethnic. Serbs began to fear retaliation from other colleagues. Serbs began to exchange opinions on how to protect themselves, and these fears were confirmed by events around Sarajevo. People convicted of serious crimes were being incorporated into the reserve police forces and MUP employees would be stopped, checked, searched, and intimidated by those forces. Tomislav Puhalac was checked in the Bistrik settlement by men in civilian clothes wearing green berets. They removed his official gun and threatened to kill him in front of his family. When reported to the Sarajevo SJB refused to take any action. It was known that the weapons were being distributed to known criminals. The Green Berets and the Patriotic League further received weapons from various other sources. Further, extremists from other parts of Yugoslavia were being employed in prominent positions in the MUP. Discrimination continued in the MUP. Serbs were demoted or reassigned and radio interception centre were moved to secret locations including private houses. The MUP failed to take action against acts committed by paramilitary organisations against civilians. It was well known who killed a Serb wedding guest in Bascarsija. However, the MUP failed to take any measure to arrest him. Only Serbs loyal and obedient to the MUP in those illegal activities could survive. All others were unprotected as there were no longer mechanisms to protect them. As a result, Serbs began to move their families to safer areas. Mr. Tomislav Puhalac moved his family in April 1992 following a shot being fired at his children's bedroom window. It was difficult to leave the town as Green Berets, the Patriotic League, and the mono-ethnic reserve forces had erected barricades on all exit routes. It also became very difficult for Tomislav Puhalac to return to work due to the barricades. One day when he did manage to return to the MUP building, he was told that the SB chief, state security chief Munir Alibabic had ordered he be prohibited from entering the building. In April 1992, the Green Berets began to block JNA barracks and commands and take over police stations. Police officers were killed and beaten of Serb ethnicity. There then followed a severe attack on the Serbian majority part of Ilidza from the Muslim majority of the town. As it was clear that a civil war had already begun, Tomislav Puhalac became a member of the national security force. Serbs were expelled from Sarajevo, their employment discontinued, and the apartments they owned or rented were broken into, plundered and subsequently given to the Muslim extremists. Many Serbs who remained in Sarajevo were tortured or killed trying to leave the town. And that is a short summary. I would like now to clarify what learned Madam Edgerton had posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalac, could you help us, please. In paragraph 2 we have the word "Sokolac" in the third -- third grammatical case. Now is this in fact -- were you trying to say here in Soko -- u Sokocu [phoen], in other words, in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's -- I just reported to the organisational units that had already belonged to the Sarajevo centre, and later on it became a department of the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please give us this word "Sokocu" in the first case, grammatical case. What is it, Sokolac? Correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, it's Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the third line from the bottom, this Lukavac or Lukavica, what is it supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Well, it's Lukavica. That is a settlement near Sarajevo. Today it is in the eastern part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please just slow down a bit and let's try and make pauses between question and answer. Now, I would also like to ask you whether you have the statement in printed form before you.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please pause. Now, please take a look at paragraph 7. In paragraph 7, you mention a name, and the statement that was taken during an investigation involving drug -- weapons trafficking. Could you tell me who the person who took the statement and who conducted the investigation were?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Well, the investigation was conducted by official police forces at the time, and the man in question is a man who illegally imported a truckload of weapons. He -- the police stopped him, checked his ID, checked the -- searched the truck, found the weapons and seized it. I had occasion to see that statement. He never denied that the weapons were imported for the need of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League in Hrasnica. This man whose name is mentioned here is otherwise from Hrasnica himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this statement taken by your service or, rather, were you up on it, did you know what it was about?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I had occasion to see the statement. It was taken by my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalac, do you hear me, Mr. Puhalac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please wait before you start answering Mr. Karadzic's question. Please put a pause for the benefit of the interpreters. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have 1D52, 1D52 in e-court, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telegraphic variant of this statement; correct? Judging by the type of the font.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I realise that, but I just wanted to gain some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalac, could you please tell us what this statement is about? What does it deal with? Could you just tell us in your own words.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just wondering about this. Is Dr. Karadzic asking him to discuss the contents of the statement based on a recollection that he's already given evidence about, or is Dr. Karadzic asking him to read the contents of the statement into the record? If this is a question based on recollection, what's the point of having the statement in front of him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness mentioned in paragraph 7, as a striking example, this case that was registered by the police, and he was in on this investigation. Perhaps my question wasn't properly put, but we have the statement in writing, the 1D55, but I just wanted to ask the witness whether this was, in fact, that same statement and how it was taken and whether he knew about it at the time when was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If Dr. Karadzic wants to establish a foundation for the witness to deal with the statement, maybe that foundation could be established properly based on the evidence that the witness gave at page 7 talking about the circumstances of the investigation, the nature of the individual's involvement, identifying the colleagues who took the statement. The witness has said he had occasion to see the statement, when that was. There are ways to go about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic should appreciate it, Ms. Edgerton. Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalac, could you assist us in this respect and tell us who it was who took the statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly the names of the people who took the statement, but I did have occasion to see it, and it was taken certainly by officials of the Ministry of the Interior. This is that statement. I recall it, although I hadn't seen it since. I haven't seen it since, but I do know that it existed and that's why I mentioned it in my statement. I also knew in person that man, and I know all of these people, and this is how things happened. It is indisputable that he was stopped and his IDs, his papers, checked and that the weapons were seized, and here we can see on whose orders this was done. So it is correct. The statement was taken by officials of the then MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D855, please. 1D855. Could we now show the following pages, the pages that follow, because there is a page in handwriting. I believe that's the fourth page. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see this version in handwriting at the time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now just leaf through it and see what it says here toward the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe Dr. Karadzic can just ask the question instead of leading the witness through the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me see. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalac, did the police where you worked at the time verify this statement on the ground? Did they check it? And was this statement -- did it reflect truthfully the acts of this man and his group?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did this affect the atmosphere within the police? What kind of ramifications did it have?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Well, this man was not held accountable for what he had done in any way, and of course among many people, professionals within the MUP, especially those of Serb ethnicity, this created disbelief and distrust and lack of faith in the MUP, the institution where we had worked until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please tender this one into evidence, 1D855?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think the evidence from the witness so far actually confirms what I had suspected, that this is a statement that falls specifically within the lex specialis, Your Honours, and is therefore, I would say, not admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think this falls into the same category that you've taken under submission last week. So perhaps you could take this under submission and we can, based on your ruling, have the good guidance as to whether these kind of statements are useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider this matter together with 1D7846, and we'll give its ruling in due course. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I might just foreshadow this now because I think it's been the subject of discussion before, but it may either refresh everyone's recollection about previous discussions or place a marker for future purposes, but should there be any consideration of admitting this, then as we've stated before, the Prosecution would then be in a position to submit many, many statements that it was not previously in a position to do because of its understanding about the rulings of a similar nature but from different persons. And also we would be submitting evidence about the nature of the interrogation processes in the RS MUP and specifically with regard to coercion, intimidation, and torture, which I think would be appropriate for the Court to be able to evaluate such statements if they were to be admitted. Again, I think these matters have been broached before, but because it seems to be on the table again, I think inexplicably, I note that once more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say one thing about the significance of the substance here of this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this document talks about a lot of other people and documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not now in the presence of the witness. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no more questions for this witness at this point in time, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you tendered only 1D588 -- I'm sorry, 855.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: 855, yeah, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not 1D52.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Mr. Puhalac, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in most part in writing, i.e., through your witness statement, and you'll now be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Puhalac.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not going to take particularly long with you, Mr. Puhalac, but there's still a few questions I'd like to ask you about some of your experiences during the war. Before we step back in time, though, are you able to -- or can you just confirm for us that in November 2012, you won the elections as a member of the SDS party for the position of president of Rogatica municipality?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So even -- your evidence in your statement was that you weren't an SDS member during the period leading up to the war, but you are an SDS member now, obviously; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Correct. I have been a member since 2008. I had never been a member of any political party previous to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just to talk very briefly about your job as a member of the National Security Services for Sarajevo, your first boss in that position was Dragan Kijac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan was in charge of that service, but there were others there that were superior to him as well within the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Dragan eventually left that office to go to Pale and take a higher position, and he was succeeded by Predrag Ceranic or Ceranic. I apologise for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who succeeded Dragan Kijac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Based on my recollection, it was Dragisa Mihic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said in your statement that you left Sarajevo on the 1st of April, 1992, so it's correct, then, isn't it, that anything that you mention in your statement about events in the city after that date are things you have no personal experience of. You only heard them from someone else; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I remained in Sarajevo until the 1st of April. After I left, we continued to monitor the situation, but prior to the 4th of April, I tried each and every day to make it back in to Sarajevo and go to work, but after what happened on the 4th of April at Vraca, I stopped trying to go back to the BH MUP. Nonetheless, throughout everything that was going on, there were quite a number of people, particularly ethnic Serbs, who were leaving Sarajevo over those days, and they would talk to us and tell us about what was going on. On the other hand, we also followed the media coverage on everything that was going on in the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean you're answering my question with a yes? Do you remember my question?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it. Did I have any first-hand experience after the 1st of April? In most cases you could say it was first-hand experience because I was directly in touch with people who were involved in those developments, and I heard their stories directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You heard them from other people; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes. From colleagues who were directly involved in those developments.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, something else I wonder if you can confirm for us. Can you confirm, based on what I read in your statement, can you confirm that from late 1991 until the war broke out in 1992, Serb policemen, including yourself, would meet to discuss the situation? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: The meetings were spontaneous. Whenever we met, we would exchange our experiences and tell each other about our anxieties and concerns for our own personal safety, the safety of our families, bearing in mind everything that we saw happening around us in Sarajevo in those days. So if your question is about whether we started meeting in an organised way, then the answer is no. It was purely spontaneous and happenstance because most of us were facing similar problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So now during those meetings, you must have reported some of the things that concerned you. My question is: Who then would you report those things to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: We didn't report that to anyone. These were spontaneous meetings, for the most part, discussions about what we could do to save our families and where to head in case unrest or riots broke out. In case the pressure increased on us, our lives and the risk to our families and our safety. Given what was happening in Sarajevo those days, it was plain for all to see that there would be problems. Many of the criminals who were known to us from before were now in the city and they were given official MUP ID.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Puhalac, I appreciate that these things must have been important to you, but I wonder if you could focus a little bit more on the questions that I'm asking. So I'll move on and I'll ask another question. Are you also, based on your position at the time, able to confirm that through the auspices of policemen of Serbian nationality arms were distributed to Serb citizens in areas in and surrounding Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Could I have the interpretation again, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question for the interpreters. Can you confirm that through the auspices of policemen of Serbian nationality arms were distributed to Serb citizens in areas in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I received no weapons myself, and I think the same applies to those of my colleagues from state security that I was in touch with, and from public security too. They received no weapons that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was: Can you confirm that through the auspices -- through the policemen of Serbian nationality, arms were distributed to Serb citizens in areas in and around Sarajevo? I wasn't asking about you or your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you claim to have some knowledge, as you've said in your statement, about Bosnian Muslim arming, but you have no knowledge of Serb police involvement in arming on the other side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No. None at all. I'm talking about Sarajevo. Until the 1st of April, I had never even left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know who Tihomir Glavas is?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, he's had, like you, a long-standing career in the police, and in 1993, he wrote a report to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and I'll show you that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's P2308, and the date is September 20th. Now, if you go over to page 2, paragraph 2, in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In that second paragraph which begins with "At the beginning of 1991" and then talks about meetings organised by Tomo Kovac who was the commander of the Ilidza police station, Mr. Glavas who authored this document says that: "Aside from the obligation that Serbs gather up and prepare for war through these meetings that took place in Dobrinja, Ilidza, and Blazuj, it was also agreed that intense activity should be undertaken to arm citizens of Serbian nationality. Armament was transported from Ravna Romanija, Pale, Sokolac, Kalinovik, the village of Nedzarici, Trnovo, the village of Tosici, Hadzici, Jusuf Dzonlagic barracks, Lukavica, and Nedzarici." So, Mr. Puhalac, Mr. Glavas, who at this time was the head of the police in Ilidza, has very detailed knowledge of Serb police involvement in arming. Now, my question is: As a member of the State Security Service whose business it was to track these things, how is it that you have no knowledge and Mr. Glavas does?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No interpretation, sorry. I didn't understand the question, because I received no interpretation. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll repeat it. Mr. Glavas, who at this time was the head of the police in Ilidza, has very detailed knowledge, as we see in this document, of Serb police involvement in arming citizens of Serb nationality. So as a member of the State Security Services, which you were, whose business it was to track these things, as you've said, how is it that you have no knowledge and Mr. Glavas does?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Glavas at some point well into the war. We first met somewhere in Ilidza when he was one of the police chiefs. I never knew him before the war. State security on the one hand and public security on the other are two different organisations, two different units. I had no knowledge suggesting what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You must remember who Tomo Kovac was. He was eventually your minister of interior, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the -- just before the end of the war. I'm not quite sure about the timing, but, yes, he was the interior minister of Republika Srpska at some point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovac gave evidence before another Chamber of this Tribunal in the case against Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin, and that's at T27121 and 27130 in the transcript of evidence in that case. And his evidence was that on 5 March 1992 in Ilidza, his forces blocked the republic staff of the Territorial Defence depot in that area, took the depot and distributed the 5- to 10.000 pieces of weapons inside. If you were so well informed at this time when you remained in Sarajevo of events in the city, how is it that you claim to have no knowledge of this significant incident?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I really had no such knowledge. I know Mr. Kovac well. We're talking about Ilidza territory here. In those days, the place must have been very difficult to reach. When we left our work in those days, we'd normally go straight home. It was difficult to organise a meeting in Ilidza in those days, and I certainly know nothing suggesting that Kovac indeed ever organised anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you must know who Momcilo Mandic was.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what was his position within the Ministry of the Interior up until the 31st of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I think he was assistant minister for crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what kind of contact have you had -- or did you have with Momcilo Mandic at that time and over the years?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Momcilo Mandic -- pardon me. So Momcilo Mandic was not involved in the spontaneous meetings you've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: For the most part those of us who worked in state security. Do you want the names of the people I was working with at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, was Mr. Vlaski involved?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: We would often meet. We used to work in the same building. We'd have coffee together. So that is the kind of meeting that I was talking about. You could say "yes" in answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No, not really. Planojevic was a low-ranking commander at the Centar police station. He's a colleague of mine from Rogatica originally and a friend of mine. We used to meet privately, for private reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you been following this trial at all, Mr. Puhalac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Momcilo Mandic came to give evidence in this trial, and Momcilo Mandic is mentioned in an interview in the magazine "Slobodna Bosna" that we're going to have a look at. That's P1113. And he gave this interview in April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S document we can go over to page 4, the bottom of the left-hand corner, and in the English document page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, under the heading in "Slobodna Bosna," under the heading that reads: "In what ways did you help the Serb side?" Mr. Mandic says: "I gave them or put at their disposal official cars, I recruited and admitted to the police force those Serbs proposed by Radovan Karadzic and Rajko Dukic, but I also gave them some material means and communications equipment. We would even deliver weapons to Serbian police stations, for example, in Pale, Sokolac, etc. We grabbed and shared out as much as was needed." Now even though you said you didn't have any contact with Mr. Mandic, here he is talking about widespread activity of arming, and we've seen that in the previous document, and talking about the delivery of weapons to Serbian police stations, Sokolac, the area where you worked, and you still claim to have no knowledge of Serb police involvement in the arming?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I do not belong to the Sokolac police station. As I said at the outset, there was a section of the State Security Service from Sarajevo there. When I left Sarajevo, I reported to that section and not to the police station itself. These are two different things. I am not saying that the police were being armed or were not being armed. Either way, I'm not saying anything. But I certainly wasn't involved in anything like that, and I never noticed anything like that going on, particularly not in relation to Mr. Mandic whom I would meet in Sarajevo. I knew what his official capacity was, and we go way back before the war because we used to go to the same school and we used to work for the same institutions. I was not a member of the police, not for a single day. I left the old state security. That's the way we called it. And then there was the public security sector or department. When the Serbian national security was set up, I became a member, but again that is a different department which is separate from the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Another thing, something I noticed you didn't mention in your statement to Dr. Karadzic, was the barracks [sic] that were erected throughout Sarajevo on the 1st and 2nd of March, 1992, but as an SDB employee at the time, I would have thought you had information about the situation. So perhaps you can confirm that both reserve and active policemen were involved in the erection of the barricades. That's the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 21, "barracks" should have read "barricades."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in fact, active and reserve -- that included active and reserve employees of the Ministry of the Interior of Serb nationality; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I -- I can't really say for certain. I can't remember a single active-duty police officer, Serb or Muslim, but there were barricades all over the place. There were a lot of police milling about. I didn't know each and every one of them, but I believe that police were involved in setting up barricades on both sides of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 65 ter 10778. It's a document dated 13 March 1992, and it's from the undersecretary of the SDB, the security forces, forwarding a list of employees of the MUP who took part in the activities relating to the setting of the barricades. Now, can we go over to page 2 in -- pardon me, can we go over to the last page of the document in both languages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, it's a one-page document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just one second.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The one I've got has several pages so if you can just indulge me a moment to check, and if we can't fix it quickly, I'll move on. Mr. Reid should be able to fix something and I'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The other thing that you didn't mention in your statement, Mr. Puhalac, is that the day before you left Sarajevo, Mr. Mandic sent a dispatch announcing the establishment of a Serbian Ministry of the Interior on the 31st of March, 1992, and the reference is P1116. He wrote to all forces on this -- on the day this law comes into force, the security services centres and public security stations of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior, are abolished and cease to function, and their authority, and he continues, is taken over by the organisational units of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, you didn't mention that in your statement, but that's actually why you left Sarajevo, isn't it, Mr. Puhalac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: There were negotiations to divide the MUP at the top of the police cadres both on the Serb and Muslim side, and among others, this was confirmed by Delimustafic during his trial. I could follow this during -- in the media. So there were negotiations to divide the MUP for the reasons that I mention in my statement and due to the events and developments. I do not know specifically of this document. I left for security reasons. I wanted to make sure that my family was safe, but as you can see from my statement, you can see that later on I did join the public security service, Serbian, later on, and I do know that there were negotiations to divide up the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You mean to say that -- well, even though you talk about negotiations, you have no knowledge of the establishment of the Serbian MUP on the 31st of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I did not take part in the negotiations myself, but I do know that there was talk about it and that there were these announcements that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So now you are conceding that you actually were informed that the Serbian MUP was established the day before you left Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: No, I was not informed, but as soon as I left Sarajevo, I learned about this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if we can go back to 65 ter number 10778, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this is the document dated 13 March 1992, and I showed this to you because you said you couldn't remember a single active-duty police officer, Serb or Muslim, involved in the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we can go over to the very last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see that it reads: "In the Crisis Staff of the SDS, among others, the following persons were engaged: Momcilo Mandic, Mico Stanisic, Dragan Kijac, Dragan Devedlaka, and Cedo Kljajic." And you said earlier that Dragan Kijac was actually your superior for a brief period of time. So here's your superior described by the vice secretary for the SDB, the vice secretary for your services, as a member of the Crisis Staff of the SDS being involved in or being engaged in the barricades and you didn't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: This document was produced at the time when Dragan Kijac was not my boss. Dragan Kijac became my boss only during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Five high-ranking members of the Ministry of the Interior, all Serb officials, one of them eventually your boss, and you maintain that you had no knowledge of Serbian police officials involved in the barricades?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I know all these men, and it is true that they were high-ranking members of the MUP, but I'm telling you Dragan Kijac was not my boss at this time. We were even employees of two different organisational units. I was with the Sarajevo centre, whereas Dragan Kijac was with the Ministry of the Interior administration and the public state security department. Now, I'm not claiming that I didn't know what was going on in Sarajevo, but I really had no -- nothing to do with the setting up of barricades in Sarajevo, nor am I aware that any of these men of the five men mentioned here participated in it, but I'm not challenging it. There are -- I even attended some meetings where there was talk about this, but I really don't know anything about it. I was not a high-ranking member of the State Security Service at the time nor a high official to be able to be privy to these conversations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, you weren't privy, you weren't privy to any inside information that you've discussed with us in your statement, were you, Mr. Puhalac, not of activities of the Serb faction or the Muslim? If we're to believe what you just said, that you were not high-ranking member of the State Security Services nor a high official. This is all second-hand information, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: If you mean the information that I provided in the statement, a lot of that has to do with events that I took part in, that I saw myself and experienced. As for the setting up of barricades, and that is what your question is about, I did not take part in that, and I did not speak either about the setting up of Muslim or Serb barricades. But I do know that I did see people and that I had difficulties because of them, but I really didn't know anything about how they were being set up, nor did I talk about that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- can we collapse the English and zoom in on the signature part. Could you help us who wrote this? Let's zoom in. The stamp. Further, further. Can you read it, Mr. Puhalac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's Branko something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this is Branko Kvesic, the undersecretary for the State Security Service. It is not quite legible, but because I see that it says there "undersecretary for the SDB," I know that Branko Kvesic was the undersecretary at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Puhalac, who is Mr. Kvesic, and when did he -- when did he join this service and when did he become its head?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Branko Kvesic was a totally anonymous person within our circles of the SDB in Sarajevo. Now he came to head the service after the elections of 1990. He was -- he's a Croat, and all I know about him is that he is from Western Herzegovina, and that at the very start of the war he himself -- and I can't tell you exactly at what time -- precise time period this was, but he and Croat cadres left the MUP together with his colleagues from Western Herzegovina. They left the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina and went to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us something about his professionalism and competence and his non-biased position vis-a-vis political parties?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, and we exchanged information of this nature, this was a political appointee. I believe that he was not an experienced state security official or operative, that he was appointed via party channels and that is how he behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he supposed to have a Serb -- a Serbian associate in this distribution of different posts --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- and offices?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: In the distribution of the posts his deputy was supposed to be a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Distribution of posts was not anything touched on in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we are talking about this document and the person who produced this document. Let us see whether the contents of this document are in fact reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Very well. Let us see. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic, but do not put the question in a leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the ethnic distribution of those posts, the managing posts, was?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: The deputy undersecretary for state security, in other words, Branko Kvesic's deputy, was supposed to be a Serb according to this distribution. However, this person was never appointed -- or, rather, just before the war, briefly Nedjo Vlaski was appointed to this post, but then, very soon, this post was eliminated because it was claimed that it wasn't necessary. At the State Security Service --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, but if it's about the document, then how about a question about the document which is a list of employees of the SRBH MUP who took part in the activities relating to the setting up of the barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This document was not tendered, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I will leave this topic then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you one more thing. After this report, was a criminal report filed against these men?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 17, you were asked about how it was possible that you didn't know anything about the arming and so on. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber where you worked and where you were appointed, in what department, before the war? How did your career evolve?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Before the war I worked in several departments of the state security department. Just before the war, a few months before the war, I was appointed to the bureau for drug fighting, so I was moved from the SDB without any official decision or any explanation. Before that, I worked in a number of departments, operative department, the operative technology and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why were you moved to the drug fighting unit?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I assume that was because the department where I had been until then knew people were being appointed, and they were simply removing the earlier professional -- professionals who worked there and appointing new people. In this way, we professionals were discredited, and we were people who still harboured the illusion that things would remain the way they had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did this reflect on your knowledge about what you were asked, namely, the arming of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: Well, there was a lot of work -- I had a lot of work in the drug-fighting department. Also, I was removed from sources and knowledge that I could access at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last question, Mr. Puhalac. You mentioned some new people coming to the department, party-appointed people. Now, did the Serbian Democratic Party appoint anyone to the high positions in the MUP or the SDB, anyone who was not an experienced MUP or SDB professional?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV PUHALAC
utterances.text: I don't know of one single instance, but also I did not have any ties with the SDS headquarters at the time, but all the men who remained on the Serb side, they were people who had worked there before and these were professionals.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Puhalac. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Puhalac, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll hear the next witness's evidence after the break, but before we adjourn for a break, I'd like to deal with a couple of matters. First, the Chamber refers to the submission of Mr. Robinson on the morning of Friday last week, where he indicated that he was not tendering a number of documents through Witness Desimir Sarenac, as he was intending to file a bar table motion at the end of his testimony to admit these documents. When questioned by the Chamber about why he didn't lead this material live with the witness during his direct examination, Mr. Robinson indicated that it would have taken an inordinate amount of time. The Chamber reiterates that it would be a matter for the Defence what strategy it would adopt, what documents it would consider significant to its case, it could present through a witness. Mr. Robinson indicated that if the documents had to be led one by one, the Defence should be granted an additional four hours. When the Chamber noted that the 300 hours granted to the accused was more than sufficient, Mr. Robinson then indicated they would be filing a bar table motion. This is not an appropriate approach. There are some items that the Chamber would like to note in that regard. Number 1, the Chamber has consistently held that the most appropriate method for the admission of a document is through a witness who can speak to it and answer questions in relation thereto and that admission from the bar table is an exceptional measure. In these circumstances where the accused has the witness on the stand who can comment on the content of documents and the accused does not want to spend his time going through the documents, the bar table motion should not be the fall-back option. This cannot be deemed a sparing or limited use of the bar table mechanism. Number 2, the Chamber notes that when granting 300 hours for his Defence case, it expected that many of the witnesses would be partial Rule 92 ter witnesses and some would be called viva voce. The Chamber has now observed that most of the Defence witnesses called have been virtually complete Rule 92 ter witnesses for whom the accused has used almost no time on direct examination. Under these circumstances, the Chamber is of the view that the 300 hours granted is actually much more than the number of hours required by the accused to present his case, and if the Defence believes certain documents are of significance, they should ensure they are probably contextualised and put directly to a witness who can comment on its contents and cannot claim that more time is required for this purpose. Number 3, the Chamber further notes that it instructed the accused on the 21st of February, 2013, that he should "focus and tender only those exhibits which are really of significance to the case against him and avoid tendering peripheral documents through 92 ter statements which he then ultimately decides not to tender or even use with the witness." The Defence should keep this in mind in preparing future 92 ter statements and notifications and should avoid tendering documents which clearly do not form an indispensable and inseparable part of the witness's evidence and statement. The accused sought to tender 230 associated exhibits with Desimir Sarenac. When this Chamber said this was an inappropriate use of 92 ter and ordered that he be led viva voce, the accused only used two documents in his direct examination, which suggests that most of the documents did not form an indispensable and inseparable part of the witness's evidence. The accused then declined to put these documents to the witness directly and then flagged the possibility of tendering these documents from the bar table. This cannot be an acceptable approach to tendering evidence in the circumstances. Next, the Chamber will issue two oral rulings on Prosecution's motion with respect to Rule 92 ter statements of Defence witnesses. First I turn to the "Prosecution Motion to Exclude in Part the Evidence of Witness Radenko Gengo," filed on the 5th of March, 2013, in which the Prosecution seeks the exclusion of paragraphs 5 to 8 of the proposed Rule 92 ter statement for Radenko Gengo. The Prosecution argues that they are irrelevant to the charges in the indictment as they pertain to actions taken by Croatian forces against the JNA. The accused opposes the Gengo motion, arguing that similar evidence has been admitted through Prosecution witnesses. Having reviewed Gengo's proposed statement as well as the parties' submissions, the Chamber is of the view that paragraphs 5 to 8 are relevant as background information to the contents in the indictment. The Chamber refers to its "Decision on Prosecution's Motion for Admission of Evidence of KDZ172, or Milan Babic, Pursuant to Rule 92 quater" issued on the 13th of April, 2010, in which the Chamber had identified in detail which Croatia-related evidence it deemed relevant or irrelevant for the purpose of this case, and in particular to paragraph 18 and footnote 31 therein. Accordingly, the Gengo motion is denied. I now turn to the "Prosecution's Motion to Exclude in Part Evidence of Witness Jovan Nikolic," filed on the 5th of March, 2013, in which the Prosecution requests that paragraphs 4 in part and 6 to 15 be excluded from Nikolic's proposed Rule 92 ter statement. The Prosecution argues that this pre-indictment information is not relevant to the charges in the indictment. The accused opposes the Nikolic motion, arguing that this information is relevant to understanding the mens rea of those individuals who may have committed crimes in the Bratunac area. Having reviewed Nikolic's proposed statement as well as the parties' submissions, the Chamber is of the view that paragraph 4 from the third sentence onwards, as well as paragraphs 6 to 15, should be excluded from the statement as they pertain to a time period far removed from the period of the indictment and have no bearing on the crimes charged against the accused. The Chamber thus grants the Nikolic motion and instructs the accused to upload a redacted version of Nikolic's proposed Rule 92 ter statement onto e-court prior to the start of his testimony. The Chamber will take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration. Mr. Avlijas, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Avlijas. Be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Avlijas, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule that we have here at the Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this Rule, Mr. Avlijas, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Avlijas.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you one thing. We have to speak slowly and make a pause between my questions and your answers. You can follow on the screen. When the LiveNote stops, that means we're ready to proceed. First of all, I would like to thank you. You are the witness number 100 in my case.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No less than I would expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you make a statement to my Defence team, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. I made two statements to your team. Was it in 1997, and the last one was last year. I made a statement to Mr. Marko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm waiting for the interpretation. I'd like you to do the same thing, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D7199 in e-court, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see on the screen the statement that you made, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're not making a pause, are you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it. I see the statement. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But what I'm saying is wait up, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read and sign this statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to the last page of the statement so the witness can see his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this statement a faithful reflection of what you told the Defence team at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were I to ask you the same questions today that you were asked at the time, would your answers in essence still be the same, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I have nothing to add or indeed to take away from my statement. I could make further comments, but in essence, yes, my answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the statement and the related documents under 92 ter, and then I will have some live questioning to conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would ask that four documents be admitted as associated exhibits. They're the first four in our list, and we would ask that they be added to our 65 ter list as they were not included in our exhibit list due to inadvertence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With the single caveat that we're looking into a translation issue with respect to one document, but that doesn't affect the issue here about associated exhibit or not, so no objection in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you'll raise the translation issue in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Or as we get it resolved with -- in due course with inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit them all. Shall we give the numbers for them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 92 ter statement 1D7199 will be Exhibit D3105, and the four documents will be Exhibits D3106 through to Exhibit D3109 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will read a short summary of Mr. Slobodan Avlijas's statement in English. [In English] Mr. Slobodan Avlijas was born on 18th of April, 1945, in the village of Rudnik, Ilidza municipality. Slobodan Avlijas held several positions within the Ministry of Justice. He officially became a member of the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War in November 1993, serving in an advisory capacity prior to this. In November 1993, he became assistant minister for justice and administration. The initial establishment of the Ministry of Justice in the new Government of Republika Srpska was difficult due to the lack of organisation and resources. The primary task of Slobodan Avlijas and his colleagues based at the Kula KP Dom was to establish a functioning judicial system. All correctional institutions during this period struggled because of the lack of funds and organisational and security problems. In mid-July 1992, Slobodan Avlijas travelled with his colleagues to Vogosca and Ilijas, neighbouring municipalities in Sarajevo, with the task of setting up a detention ward for the purposes of a lower court. Slobodan Avlijas informed authorities in both areas that the treatment of prisoners of war needed to be lawful and in accordance with international humanitarian law, pursuant to the instructions issued to the effect -- to that effect by President Karadzic. These instructions established that the corps commanders were responsible for implementing these requirements in every VRS corps. Conditions in the Kula KP Dom were acceptable. Prisoners of war were provided with food and medical services and were protected from mistreatment or physical abuse. On some occasions paramilitaries in the area attempted to harm prisoners, but all attempts were made to protect them. As a member of the Commission for Exchange, Slobodan Avlijas participated in negotiations with authorities of Herceg-Bosna which fell through because the members of the Croatian commission were only interested in exchanging five persons out of the group. Later, he was sent as a liaison officer to the French embassy and their military attache in connections with another proposed simultaneous exchange. Slobodan Avlijas also initiated meetings with authorities in Prijedor with regards the Trnopolje collection centre, who informed him that contrary to the media reports at that time, the collection centre had ceased operating. In October 1992, in response to reports that the situation in the prison -- prisons was critical, Slobodan Avlijas was assigned by the government to travel personally to the relevant areas and conduct interviews. In Vlasenica, Slobodan Avlijas saw directly that there were no prisons or prisoners. And in Prijedor and Banja Luka, he was informed that all prisoners had been transferred out of the territory of those municipalities. In Zvornik, there were approximately 60 prisoners of war whose names Avlijas noted. In Brcko, Mr. Avlijas requested a neutral international mediator to determine the identities of individuals deceased in the recent street violence. The situation in Hadzici was chaotic, and Mr. Avlijas took measures to ensure prisoners of war in the area were not made an object of reprisal by local Serbs whose families were tortured in the neighbouring Tarcin silo camp run by Muslims. In Doboj, Mr. Avlijas facilitated full access to the prison for the ICRC representatives. Slobodan Avlijas was unable to visit prisons in Sanski Most and Foca at this time because of the war. He had no access to Foca until December 1992. Communication was still severely limited, and it was clear that the War Presidency had total authority over the Foca KP Dom. It was not uncommon for local Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies to ignore the decisions of the Municipal Assemblies and the instructions from the Presidency regarding prisoners of war. Each Crisis Staff also formed their own commissions for exchange which at times operated independent of the central commission. Because of the wartime situation, Radovan Karadzic was objectively unable to control the activities of the Crisis Staffs on the ground. President Karadzic attempted whenever possible to unconditionally release civilians, ensure humane treatment and investigate any allegation of abuse, always in accordance with international law. The government took measures to prevent unlawful and private prisoner exchanges. It actively sought to prevent criminal activities committed by individuals and demanded proceedings be instigated against such persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you about your visit to Prijedor with Mr. Beat and Cedo Aleksic. What did you tell us about Trnopolje? Who set it up, and who was accommodated there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I headed for Prijedor following instructions by Mr. Momcilo Mandic. He told me that I had to submit a detailed report to both him and the government on the situation in Prijedor, specifically in relation to Trnopolje which had been dismantled already. We had been informed about that, mainly that the collection centre had been dismantled. That was at your intervention as the minister suggested, because you and Mr. Kalinic were in Geneva at a meeting at the time. At that meeting the president of the International Red Cross showed you evidence about the existence of camps and also about Trnopolje resuming operation. So I travelled to Prijedor. This was a delicate matter, and I refused to travel with no ICRC representatives present. The ICRC HQ was in Banja Luka and the representative, the person acting on behalf of that office was Mr. Beat, if I'm not mistaken. I got hold of Dr. Cedo Aleksic, who was assistant minister for health, so I asked him to come with me to that meeting. This was, as I said, a serious matter. We travelled to Prijedor and met with the local leaders, Dr. Kovacevic, Dr. Stankic, Simo Drljaca, and the president of the municipal conference of the Red Cross or whatever it was called, Mr. Srdja Srdic. We were told that the reactivation of the Trnopolje collection centre occurred because of some irresponsible individuals in Prijedor who had made Muslims organise themselves and go back to Trnopolje, upon which they would be transferred to countries in the West. When I arrived there, Trnopolje was no longer operating, and people had dispersed already. I remember that Mr. Beat, the representative of the ICRC office in Banja Luka, told the political leaders of Prijedor municipality in no uncertain terms that Trnopolje and other camps had to cease to exist in Prijedor territory. This was an unequivocal order from President Karadzic. I have to say that Srdja Srdic, a Red Cross representative, refused to obey that. He said that he was a senator in Prijedor, a deputy of the people, but his opinion was not taken on board, and the conclusion was what it was. The media were told about this, and I think that the media actually carried the reports from the meeting in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D40701, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information suggesting whether the ICRC actually allowed for these evacuations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I had nothing in writing suggesting that. Nonetheless, at the meeting, the working methodology was discussed. The Red Cross took in people who reported to them and said they wanted to go to other countries in the West, and Srdja Srdic tried to organise this for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is a Red Cross document dated the 2nd of October, 1992. It talks about the evacuation of 1.560 persons from Trnopolje. I will read to you something that it states in paragraph 2. Paragraph 2: "[In English] The people concerned were civilian victims of the ongoing hostilities in Northern Bosnia, and had all been visited and provided with assistance by ICRC delegates since the ICRC was first able to enter the camp on 10th of August. Each of them was given the opportunity to confirm that he or she did in fact wish to be evacuated." [Interpretation] How does this tally with what you found out about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Avlijas. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We go through this with every witness, so I'm going to -- I rise immediately, although if there's a redirect, I have -- I'm not confident it will be heeded, but this is another example of leading a witness through a document rather than asking the witness for information, and we -- this is persistent, and at this point incorrigible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, as Mr. Tieger indicates, you could easily put the question to the witness without having to rely on this document first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me. I thought that Dr. Karadzic actually had done that when he asked the question at line 13: "Did you have any information suggesting whether the ICRC actually allowed for these evacuations?" And then the witness answered that people had said that they wanted to go to other countries. And then having received that answer, Dr. Karadzic put the document to the witness. So it seemed to me that he was proceeding in accordance with the manner in which the Chamber had suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will withdraw it. I think the problem has been persistent, but in this case, I take Mr. Robinson's point and withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, my question: What is the relation between the text here and what you were actually told?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It's the same. It's just retold here. So information is confirmed that the ICRC and the local RC made it possible for people to fulfil their desired to leave for other countries in the West.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3110, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, in your statement you talk about the establishment of a judicial system and state organisation at my instructions. Do you remember any of these specific instructions that I issued about that at the time, or do you know pursuant to which documents that was done? When you say "Mr. Karadzic's instructions," what exactly do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: When the judicial system was first being set up, I was one of the team of people who were busy doing that, setting up courts and the like. The principle governing the application of the relevant laws was based on the laws of the formal Bosnia-Herzegovina which did not run counter to the new laws at the time. Everybody was free to make accommodations for experts to be appointed to these bodies, and this was done in co-operation with the districts and then judges were appointed at each of the levels - the Basic Court, the District Court, and then the Higher Court. At the outset there was a very good example. In Banja Luka, judges who were judges before the war belonging to other ethnic groups, Bosniaks and Croats, were also appointed. I don't know what became of it later on. That was in Banja Luka and Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to apologise to the Prosecutor at this point, because there's something that we failed to notify them about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that my instructions were followed, and both the Presidency and I were adamant that a judicial system should be set up. So my question is: Did you have any particular documents in mind when you talked about that? What exactly did you know about our positions on those issues?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: All of the positions were about obeying the law and the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this was to apply throughout the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia formally speaking, because there were laws applying throughout the former country, such as the ZKP, and all of those laws and the constitution had to be complied with and obeyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what were the instructions and the guidelines you actually received about criminal investigations and the way you treated prisoners and potential criminals?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The instructions were to do nothing that wasn't in keeping with the law, that there was some meetings with you and some people from the Assembly. I remember a specific meeting in Bijeljina, and everybody was adamant that we had to apply the law and that everything we did had to be in compliance with the law. So the citizens could feel and could see for themselves that a rule of law was enforced and that it was actually fully operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 5990. Again, my apologies to the OTP. Just to make sure what the witness really knows about the substance of this document. Could we also have the English version, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember receiving guidelines of this nature? These are of the 14th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, for the most part guidelines such as these were received by the minister of justice, and he was aware of them, and then later on he would actually brief us, the employees of the Ministry of Justice, depending on which department we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 5 in Serbian. That's chapter 6. In English that will be page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we see it reads "Tasks in the field of jurisdiction and administration." So please let's take a look at paragraph 13. Do you recall whether this was something that was presented to you and that you were -- that was set as a task?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
