utterances.text: Well, for the most part, judicial organs depending on the functions that they performed had to establish contact with the army and other individuals or persons who were charged with -- who were competent, who had authority over the prisoners or prisoners of war. And everyone in their own department would have to act, and this involved the collection of evidence so that certain people who were prisoners of war who were held captive were to be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say "persons," and here it says "perpetrators and persons," did that -- or, rather, what kind of -- how important was the ethnic background in terms of the actions taken by the judicial organs?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone and repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, could you come closer to the microphone and speak a bit more slowly. Yes. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The task of the state organs, judicial organs, and the organs of the interior was the same as it had been before the war. In other words, crime fighting, crime prevention. As you know, at the beginning of the war there was a lot of fighting. There were murders. There were a lot of detained persons because of murders they had committed. There were also robberies and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: About the ethnic background of perpetrators or victims, what was the position on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, the position was the same. A perpetrator of a crime, whether -- so a perpetrator of a crime does not have any colour or race or any ethnic background. For a really professional person, it is totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue speaking slowly if you may. We would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we see the next page in Serbian. It should be 14, although erroneously it says 13, but in English it will be on the same page. That's paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at this paragraph that relates to your ministry and tell us whether -- whether the guidelines were complied with.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Right after these guidelines were received, a commission for the investigation of war crimes that was attached to the government was established, and the way it worked -- and at the very beginning there was another commission, a Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War which worked together with other state organs, and there were counts -- they were counselled in terms of how to treat prisoners of war. They were instructed. And the very fact that I was engaged on several of the cases, I was involved in the organisation of the exchange of prisoners of war, and that very fact shows how involved the judiciary was with these problems. There was the case of an exchange with prisoners of war, Croats, and another case where Dr. Kushner was an intermediary, and in April 1993, at one point I was appointed as a member of the central Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War. Now, I was born in 1945 and not in '41. It doesn't make any sense. But what this shows is that the judicial organs and the judiciary and the MUP assisted in their -- this commission and its work, because in Banja Luka, while I worked, there was a delegated member of the Ministry of the Interior who was in charge of dealing with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did say 1945. The problem is in the translation. Now, could you tell us about this paragraph? What did it have to do with your inspections that you conducted on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, it related to that, because whenever I went out in the field pursuant to orders of the Ministry of Justice, probably the information or reports that I sent back were not at somebody's -- were not viewed positively by some people because I was -- I was -- I adhered strictly to legal precepts, and I felt that such a report could only improve the situation because there was -- there were these stories going around in the media about all these things happening, and the information that I provided about the situation in the camps, one was in Banja Luka -- the second was in Banja Luka and the third in Herzegovina, they were very well grounded. There was a lot of evidence and proof. And I also submitted some proposals because I was not authorised to issue an order. I could only state what the situation was and forward this to the minister who would then forward it to the government. The government would then adopt a position and inform you on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did people fear you whenever you showed up in the field?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, because I was very honest. I would always say what I thought. When I saw -- when I came to some of these camps and saw what a horrible situation was there and that people were held in bunkers and so on, I asked these people, "What do you think? Don't you think someone will be held accountable for this? Do you think this will go on for a hundred years? There will be people talking and writing about you've been doing here." And I sent an information to the president of the court, the supreme court and the prosecutor, and we informed them of your order or instructions 9 which was published in the Official Gazette number 9 in 1992, where it was clearly stated how prisoners of war were to be treated and who was responsible for prisoners of war and their treatment. Whenever I had the opportunity and the occasion to do these inspections on the ground, I would advise them of the International Law of War and international regulations that had to be complied with. I knew of all of these conventions. I knew how much air or how much food these people who were held as prisoners of war needed according to these international norms, so I would always tell them whenever I visited these people on site, I would advise them thereof. Now, as for your guidelines, they stated that it was important to determine exactly who it was who was held as prisoner of war and that these people should be categorised because this was a burden to every society. You had to care for their clothing, for their food and so on, and this in itself --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last portion of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters were not able to hear the last portion of your answer, Mr. Avlijas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last thing I mentioned had to do with one -- had to do with one of the paragraphs in your guidelines where I said that they had to take care of all the prisoners of war, that triage had to be conducted so that we knew exactly who belonged to what category, who -- what category of imprisoned or detained persons there are. And I especially pointed out that it was very bad for our image if we had a lot of prisoners of war and also that it was a very sizable expense that society had to incur for taking care of these people and for these detention centres and keeping them as they should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what was the position of the central authorities, the government and the Presidency, vis-a-vis your work on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I can say when I prepared these reports that I was a bit fearful, because I was very objective. There were even -- there were even suggestions by some of my associates that I was very brave, but I have to say that I have never received any complaints about my reports from anyone, the government, the military authorities, or the Presidency, and I'm proud of it because the information that I had, the raw materials that I provided, they would actually be accepted by all these three levels without any comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last question: Although you were not authorised to issue orders, did the situation improve on the ground -- or, rather, what was the position of these organs in the field before -- even before they would receive some order from the ministry?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, the information certainly improved, and I have to mention the case of Bileca where people really took it seriously, and persons who had been isolated before that, and I wouldn't want to go into a discussion about terminology, what a detained person actually means, but I can give an example, a good example of how local authorities took steps and they make -- made a good assessment of how to do it in order to protect the unprotected Muslims. There were -- there was -- there were uncontrolled elements of the military and paramilitary groups that all headed in that direction. The president of the municipality at that point and his aides, because in the meantime the mosque had been blown up, collected all the Muslim male population and put them in a student hall where they provided their accommodation, enough air. They were provided with food that was brought from their homes, and then the Presidency did -- made a great effort to ensure that those people were moved to a secure -- to a safe place because there was a huge number of these uncontrolled elements that had come to that area, and it was hard to guarantee their safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where Zelenika is, where these people were moved for safety?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Zelenika is a small harbour between Herceg Novi and Kotor in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the effect of your inspections conducted in -- of your inspections in Sarajevo municipalities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to go over what I've already said, but when I was ordered to go to Vogosca on the 12th of July, 1992, the president of the corps, Milenko Bjelica, the municipal prosecutor Milorad Panjevic, and representatives of the Ministry of Justice talked about Vogosca. Now, as I've already said, there were people who were kept detained there. They were detained in Svrake and Vogosca, but they were held in an open-air space near a German bunker, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I please ask you -- what we have in the statement is not really necessary to repeat, but what didn't make it into the transcript is that you said that these were prisoners who had been captured during fighting in Semizovac and elsewhere. But could you just tell us what the repercussions were or what the effects were, and what was the situation in Sonja, the Sonja restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, Sonja was not really a bunker. It was more a headquarters, sort of offices, and I didn't find any detained persons there, but the effect of my -- of our meeting was that a proper and appropriate installation was found. It was a four-storey building. It was light, there was enough light, and this was the building that was used or selected to house these people, the detainees, and this covered the area of three or four municipalities in that region. Now, when I selected this building as an investigating prison, then they asked me when we went and saw this, they asked me, "Is this the kind of building that you would like to use?" And I said, "Yes." And then that's what they did. But the same thing happened in Ilijas where people had been held in some kind of warehouse, but after our intervention and suggestion, these people were moved to and accommodated in an appropriate -- to appropriate facilities which would meet certain international rules and requirements. Now, in Hadzici, there was also the case of individuals who had been returned after an exchange of prisoners fell through. The exchange of prisoners went on late into the night, so for security reasons they -- these people could not be taken back to where they had been, so they were taken to a gym in Hadzici. Now, I intervened upon this, saying that the conditions were not appropriate there, but also there was a lot of fear that the local population of Pazarici and Tarcin and Hadzici were held, detained, in the silo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests that the witness repeat his answer. He's speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas. Mr. Avlijas, you are speaking too fast, and they were not able to catch up with you, your speed in particular. Could you repeat from the part when you referred to silo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Okay. Well, I've already said a group of prisoners of war of Muslim ethnicity who were held in Kula and -- they were sent to Kobiljaca for an exchange. Now, this exchange fell through because the Muslim side obstructed it. Now, the prisoners, in terms of the locality where they were supposed to be taken back, and that's about 150 kilometres away, were moved to a sports hall in Hadzici where -- from where they had been taken a month earlier from Kula or so. A month or two. I'm not sure. Now, when I went to inspect these facilities and -- and prepare the report, I found these prisoners of war who had not been exchanged, although half had been, and they were housed in very poor conditions. They slept on the ground, on thin mats, gym mats. Now, because this municipality was divided into two parts, the part under Muslim authority and the part under Serbian authority, there was a camp in Tarcin where a lot of Serbs were held prisoner, and I was afraid that there would be a back-lash because of these people, the family members of the people who were held in that camp, the Serbs, that they would retaliate against the people held at the silo. So I intervened, and I effectuated, effected, these people being transferred to better premises, to Kula or some place like that, where they would be properly guarded and secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In addition to Kula, you also mentioned Planina Kuca, but that did not make it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, and I have no further questions for this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you put this document, you told us that this document was 14th of July, 1992. How do we know that, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Prosecutor marked it in e-court as such, but in the preamble we see that all the dates precede the 14th, or, rather, according to the Official Gazette where they were published, the regulations that this document relies on. But the Prosecutor marked it as a document of the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So bear in mind that you are not giving evidence. So date is not clear on its face on this document. If you think the date is important, you need to put that to the witness. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it here. We probably need the cover page which was not in e-court. At least I couldn't find it. But there probably was a cover page that bore this date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. So I'll leave it at that and we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3111, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, as you have noted now, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in its most -- in most part in writing in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you'll be cross examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, if I could begin, please, by just clarifying one thing you noted at the beginning of your testimony when Mr. Karadzic asked you about statements you had given. I believe you said you'd given two statements, and a date was given in 1997, and then one to Mr. Marko. So I just wanted to clarify exactly how many statements you gave to the Karadzic Defence team and when you gave them.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The Defence team of Dr. Radovan Karadzic, I only gave one statement to them. But I was also questioned, interviewed by the representatives of The Hague Tribunal at Pale in 1997. So perhaps that's where the confusion is coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think that's right, and I think now everyone understands what you're referring to of all the participants who have those documents. Thank you. Mr. Avlijas, I want to also confirm quickly that you have testified previously in different venues. You testified in the case of Stanisic and Zupljanin here in 2010. You testified in the case involving Mr. Mandic before the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 2007, and you testified in the case involving Mr. Lalovic in 2009. That's correct, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and I say so in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I presume that your position is that you gave truthful testimony in all those cases; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Maybe I commented a bit more in one or the other, but in essence all my statements are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now -- and I mention that at the outset for a couple of reasons. I am likely to be referring to portions of the information you provided previously, and I mention that now in the same spirit that Mr. Karadzic mentioned a couple of times, that it was not necessary to repeat the information you already provided to this Court in the form of your written statement. So references that I may make to portions of your previous testimony should not be understood as an invitation to repeat that testimony, but I'm simply trying to find the fastest route to getting the maximum information to the Court by pointing you to certain excerpts and having you confirm them. Understood?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, your statement mentions that you became a member of the Commission for Exchange in April of 1993, after having been initially asked in 1992 and then deferring for the reasons you describe; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I understood from your testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case that during the course of your work on the Commission for Exchange, you worked with Mr. Amor Masovic. And indeed you describe a story to the -- or you described a story to the Stanisic and Zupljanin Chamber about Mr. Masovic risking his life in the course of an attempted exchange and being assisted by a counterpart on the Serbian side, and then indicated that, "According to me, Mr. Masovic is a highly professional official." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in that exchange at the time. This is what I referred to about the exchange that fell through at Kobiljaca, because neither Masovic nor the group of Muslims who had been taken prisoner could be exchanged. They were taken to Hadzici, and Masovic slept at Brane Mijatovic's place, who was a commander of the police, and the rest were taken to the gym. As for Masovic, the co-operation between the two of us during the war was at a fairly high professional level. When I was a commission member after the war, I don't think it can be described as such. I don't know if it's relevant, but it was not a professional relationship at the time because we were unable to get -- to get our executed people because of obstruction. If the Court so wishes, I can say more about this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. No, I think that's not necessary for my purposes. I simply wanted you to confirm that you had told the Stanisic-Zupljanin Chamber, and that would be at page 155 -- 15652 and at page -- well, I'll wait. We need to get there for the e-court page. That you volunteered during the course of that testimony when you mentioned his name as the president of the commission. The question was he became rather famous, and you said: "And so we co-operated. I was a member of the Republika Srpska Commission for Co-operation, and according to me, Mr. Masovic is a highly professional official." That's at 15652, e-court page 94. Do you need to see that, or can you just confirm that for me that that was your testimony in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I stand by that statement when I refer to the period from 1992 until 1999, or actually during the war, but since his behaviour after 1996 is not relevant here, I won't go into that. He was highly professional and co-operated with us well. We exchanged information, and I really cannot say anything that is false here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. At paragraph 18 of your statement, Mr. Avlijas, you provide the following information about Mr. Skiljevic. So that's after the discussion about coming to Kula in your professional capacity and talking about circumstances at Kula, and you say: "I remember that on one occasion a member of a tank crew," and then you describe what Mr. Skiljevic did. So I wanted to clarify, Mr. Avlijas, a number of things, but beginning with this paragraph, that -- in fact, this is not something, despite the preceding paragraphs, which indicate your presence at Kula, that you saw yourself. This is you repeating an anecdote or story that you had heard; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. No, that is not correct. I stated that at the trial of Skiljevic and Lalovic too. I wanted to corroborate or show the conditions under the -- which the penitentiary facility functioned, because before the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, sorry. I'm not asking you for your motives in making the statement or testifying about it at the Lalovic case. Let's just take all this one step at a time. So now that you mentioned the Lalovic case, let me take you to your testimony in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's found at 65 ter 24743. At English page 28, and B/C/S page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there you said, Mr. Avlijas: "I remember an anecdote regarding Soniboj. Reportedly, a tank driver directed its tank almost directly towards -- then whether somebody got killed or what happened, allegedly Soniboj stood in front of the tank and said, 'You'll have to kill me,'" and then go on. So in the Lalovic case, Mr. Avlijas, you referred to an anecdote. You described it as allegedly and reportedly. That reflects something that you heard from other people, correct? And that's what you testified to in the Lalovic case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Let me correct myself. Somebody misinterpreted that. We can't speak of an anecdote here. It's a tragedy, rather, because that tank crew member had somebody killed on at that day. And I'll only try to show what things were like in the penitentiary facility. The tank driver started his tank, and then this man stood in front of the tank and said, "You first have to kill me." And those persons at Kula were not separated from us. Their building was next to ours. Where we ate, they ate. And I think it was a translation error. In my statement I wanted to show the professional attitude of the warden of the penitentiary facility toward the inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. We have your answer, sir. Let me turn to another part of your statement, and that would be a number of paragraphs dealing with access or communication with or contact with Foca. So at -- that's paragraphs 33, 35, and 60 of your statement, where you say, for example, in paragraph 35: "Previously no one from the" -- referring to December 1992. "Previously," that is prior to December 1992, "no one from the central government could get in touch with the warden of Foca." You say at paragraph 33: "The first time we were able to go to Foca was in December 1992," and you say something to similar effect in paragraph 60. Now, let me ask you first about things you may not be familiar with. Were you aware of the extent to which the Assembly of Republika Srpska was receiving information about the situation in Foca, either from members of the Bosnian Serb leadership such as Dr. Karadzic at the 16th Assembly session or from the representatives of Foca such as Mr. Maksimovic and Mr. Cancar during the course of 1992? Did you know that was happening, that they were reporting to the Assembly what was happening in -- various aspects of what was happening in Foca?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I was not in such a position as to be informed about these things. I was a mere coordinator, so I can't answer your question. I really didn't know whether information was submitted or what kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me turn to something a little closer to home, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 17213.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a request from the president of the government, Dr. Djeric, to the Crisis Staff of Foca on the 23rd of May, 1992, asking for Veljko Kostovic to came to Pale regarding the editing of the Official Gazette. So do you claim that you were not aware of contacts between the government and Foca during this period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I reiterate, sir, that I had nothing to do with the government. I know Veljko Kostovic and Branko Djeric. I know what they did. If this document is in existence, then things must have had -- must have been happening this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness hasn't said anything to this document, and it can't be something the witness could be -- could have been expected to know about such that it would be admitted as being contradictory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's -- that's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Contradictory to what, Mr. Tieger? Is it communication --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: To the claim -- to the lack of communication claim. And this is -- this is related to the government which includes the Ministry of Justice for which this witness was a high-ranking official.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, he said in line 24, page 61, that he didn't know. He hasn't said that there was no co-operation. He said he didn't know. So in order to contradict that, the Prosecution would have to show some document that would make it likely that he did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- pause. Pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. The witness cannot insulate himself from impeachment by hiding behind a general denial and claim therefore that documents that show the contrary of what he's asserted in his statement should not be admitted. This witness went to great pains and the Defence took great pains to include in the statement his assertions about the lack of communication and contact with Foca. This document proves the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was this document communicated to Foca?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would say at a minimum, Mr. President, this document certainly reflects an expectation on the part of the government that they are in contact with Foca, and it's a routine -- it's a document sent routinely with the expectation that it will be received and acted upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We do not know how this was delivered, hand-delivered, by telex or whatever. Did the witness say that total communication was cut off?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this can obviously go to weight and that's going to be one of a number of pieces dealing with this subject. But a routine request in May on a fairly simple matter certainly reflects a state of affairs that is incompatible with what the witness suggested in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean this situation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P6194, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6194.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Avlijas, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to comment on the whole situation irrespective of the document. In the month of May, but I don't remember so very clearly, how communication went. You could send a document by courier or to cover the work obligation of Veljko Kostovic in Foca, but we cannot say from this perspective that we had an organised state. There wasn't even mail delivery --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that was organised, let alone anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I let him continue. That's sufficient, Mr. Avlijas. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, do you claim you were unaware of the fact that on the 4th of July, 1992, the government adopted a decision on the founding of KP Dom Foca? That's P1098.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It would be less than serious if I said I didn't know. Yes. I even made a draft but the problem is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Avlijas. That's -- I asked you about -- I gave you the -- I suggested to you earlier how I intended to proceed, and I would also add it's not an invitation for you to argue your position. You've stated the facts as you claim they were in your statement and previous testimonies. Do you claim you were unaware that on the 3rd of June, 1992, at a government session, the government received a report on the official visit to, among other places, Foca? And that's D415.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: On the 3rd of July, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That would be 3 June, I believe. D14 -- 415, rather.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I don't know who could have been there. I had only been appointed on the 28th of May. It was in late May that I came from Ilidza where I had lived and only started working on the 28th of May, so I cannot have any knowledge about that. I really couldn't even physically be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about something about a little bit closer to home then. In the Stanisic-Zupljanin case at page 15576, you spoke about a visit to Trebinje in late June 1992 that you made as part of a justice ministry working group with three other persons, and those persons included Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Branka -- Ms. Branka Mandic, and Igor Velasevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Velasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there you testified that Mr. Nikolic and you visited Herzegovina and Trebinje, "whereas the other two went down to Foca"; correct? And that's in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And they produced the following report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 16255, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. We go to the -- all right. That report refers to the activities related to organising judiciary institutions. It says the working group of the Ministry of Justice visited Foca on 24 and 25 June 1992, talks about those with whom they held a meeting including the president of the Executive Board, the president of the various courts and judges, the warden of Foca correctional institution, and the representatives of the Ministry of the Interior in Foca. And if we turn the page so you can see the signators and signatures. It indicates Branka Mandic and Igor Velasevic. That's the report that was produced in late June 1992, as a result of the trip by the working group by the -- by the justice ministry group to Foca; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: That's correct. I have no objections. The report was submitted. They went to Foca by way of Niksic and we went to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you also make some similar -- some strong claims about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would tender the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6195, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, you also make various claims about Crisis Staffs in the course of your statement. Now, reports from Crisis Staffs to Mr. Karadzic or other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership were not intended to go through you, were they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I think that there's a misunderstanding. When I went out to the field, I had nobody to communicate with other than the president of the Crisis Staff, the chief of police, or some other --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Avlijas, you may misunderstand my question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: -- responsible person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand on the occasions that you went to the field which you indicated in your statement that you had certain reporting responsibilities and that information from Crisis Staff members could be communicated to the leadership through you, but I'm asking you as a more general matter. You were not part of the communication chain from all the Crisis Staffs in all the municipalities to the Bosnian Serb leadership; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with respect to those Crisis Staffs that you did not visit, you were not familiar with the composition of its membership; correct? You didn't know who all were on there? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. I think there's been a misinterpretation of my statement. I had nothing to do with Crisis Staffs. I didn't know who was on the Crisis Staff. But when I arrived in the field, I would ask who the president of the Executive Board was and who the president of Crisis Staff was, and I applied for a meeting with them and said that I had been sent by the Ministry of Justice to make a snapshot of the situation in Brcko, for example. There was Vojan Belok [phoen] and Djordjic as the president of the Crisis Staff. "Gentlemen, I have horrible information. Tell me what's going on in the field." And this is all the communication I had. I had no contact with the Crisis Staff, because due to the position I was in, I couldn't have had. And this is where the misunderstanding arose. Depending on the situation, who I was able to find as a counterpart to talk to in the field. For example, in Zvornik there was Mr. Lokancevic who was the chief of police, a great professional, and he said that he had 50 prisoners and that they had to be saved, and I sent the list to the government and we were able to save them. But it was different everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's talk about some of your contacts, then, in places where Muslims and Croats were being held, and let me begin with Vogosca and Ilijas, which you've -- which appear in your statement and which you've referenced today as well. Now, let me ask you about the genesis of that visit. First of all, as you testified in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case, "There were all sorts of stories in the media." That's found at 15585. Can you confirm -- and you said that those were "bad stories," at 15586. Can you confirm that that was your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. That was one of the conditions because of those rumours, and in order to implement the orders received, we had to go there and check what was situation was like in Vogosca in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And more specifically, you testified --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript does not contain anything of the witness's statement that it should contain. The witness said that the rumours about the non-implementation of the instructions of the Ministry of Defence and the president were the reason to go to the field to Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think witness is talking about his statement. He confirmed what Mr. Tieger referred to. Why don't we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm simply focusing now on what you said before about what triggered your trip. So you said in Stanisic-Zupljanin that the information in the media was that "a large number of people have been captured, that there were no conditions to hold them, and ... mass liquidations." That's at 15586. And you said further, basically everybody knew about those allegations or stories. And that's found at the same page. These true. That's the testimony you had in Stanisic-Zupljanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I think we must distinguish they didn't know what was happening, but everybody had heard the rumours that there were camps in Vogosca and that people were being tortured there, because the media of Bosnia-Herzegovina insisted on that, that there were killings and so on. And then a commission was appointed consisting of three members to go out there and see what things were like, and I can confirm today that the prisoners were held in unsuitable conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll talk about that in just a moment. And as a result there was pressure, as you testified in the Mandic case, pressure "from the International Red Cross and the public"; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, the International Red Cross constantly visited camps and penitentiary facilities. They informed the state organs, and the state organs then passed on information to the line ministries and assigned tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, I'm asking you what you testified to in the Mandic case was that there was pressure from the International Red Cross and the public. That's what you testified to; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, when you went to Sonja's in Vogosca, you went to meet with the leaders of the Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. If necessary, I can name all those present and the date. There was Rajko Koprivica, the president of the Assembly. Then the president of the Executive Board, Svetozar Stanic, also known as Sesa. There was a representative of public security by the name of Blagovcanin, I think, and the pre-war petty offence judge Mr. Lokota [phoen] and some other people. The meeting was opened by the president of the Assembly, and the introduction on behalf of the working group was given by Milenko Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The transcript didn't catch of the name of the representative from the MUP, the representative from the SJB, and that was Branko Vlaco; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No, no. Branko Vlaco represented the camp. I forgot to say that. And the representative of public security was Blagovcanin, because Branko Vlaco was in charge of the camp that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He was also from the -- he's also a member of the MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know who he was employed by. I can't say for sure whether he was working for MUP or for somebody else. Only the relevant authorities that he was being employed by can tell you that or perhaps it was a so-called work obligation too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. It's 12.30 now, the customary time for our break, Mr. Avlijas. I'll leave it to the Court, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You were not heard, Mr. Karadzic, because of overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 25 reads as if it were a question whereas actually it's part of the answer. So the Q should be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be corrected in due course. Thank you. We'll take a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, we're still discussing what you observed in Vogosca. I know you've alluded to the conditions at the bunker, but I want you, for more specificity, to confirm what you've testified to in previous cases, and in particular the Mandic case where you stated it was "truly horrific," and said that even talking about it 15 years later, "I am still horrified," and said further, "the situation was disastrous. As a normal human being, when I saw the horror there, what else could I say?" Those references are found at pages 7 and page 32 of the English. Can you confirm that was your testimony in the Mandic case, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by that statement which I repeated in the Stanisic case, the Zupljanin case, and whenever anyone cared to ask I said that this was inhumane behaviour which left me feeling horror.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the location of the bunker in relation to where you and the leaders of the Crisis Staff, including Koprivica and Stanic and others, was, as you explained in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case, about the same distance as from the witness chair to the door in the courtroom; correct? That's found at page 15590.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The meeting was held in that room and that was the distance. As for the Crisis Staff, it should have been in Vogosca but the meeting that we had was held at the Sonja cafe which was right next to the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you have also testified previously about who ordered the detentions of these people in the bunker, and as you said repeatedly in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case, and I'll ask you to confirm that, you said at page 1 -- pages 15595 through 96: "The Crisis Staff did," and then went on to explain, "I suppose they did it most likely together with the army because they couldn't do it on their own." Asked again to clarify the question about -- the question was who made the decision to take people prisoner and to put them there. You said: "The Crisis Staff did, and the army command most likely." And then again, just a few lines later, you said: "Most likely it was the Crisis Staff and the Tactical Group command that were in charge of that issue." And can you confirm that that was your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my testimony. One thing I'd like to add, the commander of the Tactical Group in terms of his position was also a member of the Crisis Staff, but I can't be certain. It's merely an assumption on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you were also asked whether the people in the bunker, the prisoners, were civilians or combatants, and you said in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case that the leaders of the Crisis Staff told you: "They told us that those were people who had been taken prisoner in areas where there were armed conflicts." And then you said further: "They told us that those people had been taken prisoner during combat." And that's at 15597. And then you went on to say: "That's what they told us. We didn't check whether those people were really combatants or not, but it was the corps commander who was in charge of making that decision." And that's at 15597. Again, sir, can you confirm that was your testimony in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by that. When I mentioned the corps commander, I meant the instructions issued by the military minister. The corps commander would be responsible for any treatment of POWs in his area, in the area under his command, and then by -- by virtue of the same principle also his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when asked whether you considered it part of your responsibility to determine whether people in the bunker were being held illegally, that is, whether they were civilians or combatants, you said: "No. Our task was to see whether there were any prisoners and where they were kept. Now, as for the procedure, our -- the legality and lawfulness of that issue, this is something that came under the jurisdiction of the army." That is what you testified to in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case, sir; correct? You told -- you said essentially it was not your job.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No objections. No objections. That wasn't our task nor, indeed, were we able to categorise. This is a purely military issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And not your job as you saw it; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No, not our job. It wasn't for us to do. Our task was only to make sure international standards were being complied with in terms of POW treatment under the relevant international conventions and law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, subsequently, as you alluded to in your testimony, a remand prison was established at Planina Kuca or Planjo's house, and the inmates at the bunker were transferred there; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: There is one thing that we need to clarify here, if I may. We had three tasks to carry out in Vogosca. One was to see what the situation was of the POWs and whether the instructions and orders of the president and the military minister were being applied. The other thing was to find a suitable facility to set up a remand unit for the regular court which had nothing to do with the prisoners. So you need to distinguish these two things, the prisoners on the one hand and the people being prosecuted according to regular procedure. All right. Once we had found a good building to set up a remand prison in which had very good access, it was fully functional and so on and so forth, then they asked us about our criticisms in terms of where they were keeping people. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, please --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Should we also transfer all of the other prisoners to that building over there --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I have limited time. That's in your statement and you also explained it during your examination-in-chief, so --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. It was the Ministry of Justice that took over control of Planjo's house sometime in July. You testified to that in Stanisic-Zupljanin; correct? Mr. Avlijas, I don't want the whole story. I am going through this step-by-step through this thing so you'll see where I'm going. If you can confirm that, please do; if you can't, I'll direct you to the page where you address that issue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice took control or became responsible for Planjo's house sometime in July; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, about the security of people being investigated and the prisoners who received their food there. Everything else was under the military, the exchanges of people being taken to work and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Brano Vlaco, the man who is responsible for the bunker, the truly horrific place that you testified about, was appointed as the warden of the detention department of the penal and correctional facility Butmir, Ilidza; correct? And that's what you testified to in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case at 15607.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. It wasn't Butmir. It was the remand prison covered by the Ilidza Basic Court, and it was at Planjina's tower in Semizovac where the other people were also being kept, the prisoners. So it was both in the same place, the remand prison and the prisoners, and Vlaco was put in charge of that facility and the business there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for the clarification. And in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case you were asked to explain why, as it was put there, why this appalling -- whether or not you had told Mr. Mandic before the appointment that the bunker had been under the control of Vlaco and your answer was: "He was probably better known than myself. Everybody knew who Vlaco was." That's at transcript page 15608. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you were asked to explain or you went on to explain -- you just went on yourself to explain everybody knew who Vlaco was. Then you started to talk about personnel policy that resulted in his appointment. And you said: "Personnel policy in the field was in the hands of the Crisis Staff and the Serb Democratic Party." And then the question was: "Right." And then you said again: "It's a well-known fact." That's what you testified to in Stanisic-Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you also went to Ilijas during that same visit, in fact during that same day, and you mentioned already that you found prisoners there who were in a warehouse of sorts, and I'm just going to clarify based on your previous testimony what conditions were like in that facility. You testified that the warehouse was packed and, further, that everybody was in civilian clothes. Both of those things are correct; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Correct. What I could see through a window. The warehouse was packed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you also testified that a number of the people there recognised you because of your pre-war position and that the meeting -- or that the encounter with them was "really emotional." That's what you said in the Mandic trial. And you said further: "They recognised me and they turned to me for help. They said, 'Slobo, how are you?'" And then you testified further: "It's an awful situation to have people begging you for help because they felt there was no hope for them." That's what you testified to in the Mandic case about your encounter at the warehouse in Ilijas; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It's true but my statement was not complete. I said there was an assumption, an agreement, that there would be an all-for-all exchange sometime soon. That was in order to give them hope. And indeed there was a lot of activity going on in order to organise an all-for-all exchange at the time. I told them that I'd spoken to people from the Ilijas authorities to make sure that appropriate accommodation could be found that would constitute an improvement over what they had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as you testified to in the Mandic case, you went to Ilijas, you met first with the president of the Crisis Staff Ratko Adzic who had basically brought his entire group with him; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: What do you mean? A group of associates, people who worked with him; right? Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And again you referred to the hope for exchange and that you mentioned to those people and the way you put it in the Mandic case was that in order to comfort these people, you told them about the possibility of an all-for-all exchange in which case "You could get out of this hell." Right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. When you talked about comforting those people, I wanted to relieve them of the burden of the hell they were suffering at the time, but if you look up existing documents on both sides, you could tell that there was a lot of activity being organised in terms of an all-for-all exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter did not understand the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There's some portion of your answer that the interpreters did not get, Mr. Avlijas, although it -- I can't figure out what might be missing because the answer does look coherent.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I wanted to say that the word that I used at the time in terms of comforting them, giving them hope, telling them what I knew, but talks were underway, large-scale important talks about an all-for-all exchange on both sides, prisoner exchange, all for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The transcript did catch that. And once again, as it had been the case in Vogosca, you didn't know whether these people were civilians or not. In this case in Ilijas, you were told -- you learned that the population -- here's what you said. Apparently that population was captured during combat. That's what you said in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case based on what you were told by the Crisis Staff; correct? And that --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. And that you didn't know whether that was true or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I didn't know whether that was true or not but I knew there was fighting going on in Ljesevo, Podlugovi and Luka, Muslim-populated villages. I made that assumption and I also knew some people who were from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to the next visit to the field which is reflected in your statement, and that was the trip to Herzegovina on the 18th or -- through the 20th of August which is referred to at paragraph 57 of your statement, and I understand from your statement that that was the first time that someone from the central government visited the collection centres. It says: "This is the first time that someone from the central government visited the collection centres and at the intervention of the president of the republic." Now, I asked you before about the impetus for your visit to Vogosca and Ilijas. In this case, you refer to this as being part of the activity that is reflected in paragraphs 54 through 57 in the -- beginning in the early part of August 1992; correct? So you refer in paragraphs 54 through 57 to the Presidency and government meetings concerning categorising prisoners and then you go on to talk about your tasking in Herzegovina. And all of that, Mr. Avlijas, was the result, was it not, of the international outcry that followed the media entry into Omarska and Keraterm and the publicising of stories and photographs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I can't say really whether that was due to any pressure from the international community. I was not a high-ranking political leader in Republika Srpska. I know that I carried out tasks given to me by my minister who in turn was given these tasks by the government or the Presidency. I had a job to do and we were also told there was pressure being exerted on the leaders of Republika Srpska and all sorts of things happening all over the place. Among other things, in my testimony I talked about a specific example, pressure being exerted in Geneva on President Karadzic and Dragan Kalinic. Pressure because there were stories circulating that there were camps around that were being set up again and still operating. And then after that, there was this government initiative to set up groups that would be sent to the field to investigate the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your statement, Mr. Avlijas, also suggests that not only was that the first time that someone from the central government went out to the camps, but that until then, you said: "We did not have any information about the events that took place the length and breadth of Republika Srpska." Now, this Court has received evidence, Mr. Avlijas, from a number of sources, among other things, a letter that deputy or assistant minister of the MUP Tomo Kovac wrote to the president and the prime minister on August 8th noting that people were not being properly categorised, including civilians, and proposing that the status of these people be changed to comply with international law. Were you -- that was -- were you aware of that letter by Mr. Kovac and that position? And that's by the way P1100.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The first I hear of Mr. Kovac's letter, but on that same subject, if I may, I could perhaps provide a comment. There was a meeting in Banja Luka in August 1992. The vice-president of the government, Milan Trbojevic, myself and Mr. Zupljanin were adamant at that meeting that one should check the camps to see who was a prisoner, who was not a prisoner, who was responsible, who was to be prosecuted, and who wasn't, that there should be a triage. So that was one of the conclusions reached at the Banja Luka meeting. As for Mr. Kovac's letter, I can't say I ever heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And your minister, Mr. Mandic, was shown this letter during the course of his testimony before this Court and stated that he considered it hypocritical because Mr. Kovac was well aware of this -- was well aware before this of the situation he described. And Mr. Mandic went on to explain that such information was received on a daily basis. So were you -- do you claim that you were not privy to the regular information about the problem with civilians in camps and categorisation that Mr. Mandic testified about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I was not privy to that. It wasn't the nature of my work. This wasn't one of my daily dealings. It was only occasionally whenever a problem cropped up because of the nature of my work, because of my natural eloquence and my knowledge of the subject, the minister would appoint me as a member of the commission who would be sent out into the field, not because I had anything to do with the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event you did go to Herzegovina as you indicated in your statement and alluded to during your examination-in-chief. Now --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Just to answer that question, I went to Herzegovina because that was decided by the Government of Republika Srpska. They appointed a commission that was sent out to investigate the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Earlier in your -- is this -- this document which was previously 65 ter 11044 and was -- is an associated exhibit, this is headed "To the Government of Serb Republic, report," and starts: "According to the decision of the Government of the Serb Republic, Slobodan Avlijas and Goran Saric were appointed to visit places in SAO Herzegovina," and we see your signature and Mr. Saric's signature on the back. But this -- this is -- this is the report; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And there's no other report about what was happening in Herzegovina about the camps, this was it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before I move on from there, I just wanted to ask you one question about one part of this report because you referred to it earlier and that's your visit to Bileca, and you stated that you were told by authorities there that all the male Muslims had been gathered up and were being -- for their safety; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And yet, Mr. Avlijas, these -- I'm going to suggest to you, as the Prosecutor in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case did, that that is not compatible with two things. First of all, you recommended, as it says here in the report, that the people over the age of 60 should be released. And as the Prosecutor in Stanisic-Zupljanin asked you, if they were being -- if they were there for their safety, why would you recommend that the most vulnerable among them be sent out and exposed to danger?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: There was probably a misinterpretation of the reports, because in -- when I visited these places I also introduced the conventions. I told them about the conventions and the provisions of the conventions that elderly and women and children are not to be detained, because that's probably where this arises from, this misunderstanding, because wherever I went I always said, "Gentlemen, you just must know one thing. You are not allowed to detain people over 60 years of age, women or children."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not much room for misunder --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: And if I may just add one thing. Perhaps the best commentary on the situation in Bileca is something that the people who were detained there could provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And also with respect to the safety issue, as you testified in the Lalovic case, the wives of those men in the -- who were being -- it says here accommodated at the SJB -- who were there at the SJB were still out in -- in the communities, completely exposed to the danger that these -- that all the men who had been rounded up were supposedly being protected from; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, that is your assessment. Few people would target women. What they -- they were looking for men. Paramilitaries when they recruited they looked for men, but there was also -- it was much easier to protect women than men, because I remained there and talked with those people. I spent an hour and a half there to talk to the people, ask them about their problems, to put them in touch with their families. I asked them whether they had ever been mistreated, whether they had enough food, and no one complained, not one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's move on to your next visit to the field and that was the trip that you took to various places culminating in the report of the 22nd of October, 1992. Now, again I want to ask you about the impetus for that meeting and, as you testified in Stanisic-Zupljanin, there was pressure after a meeting in Geneva from the -- in this case the ICRC; right? Well, you think the ICRC but you mentioned specifically Madam Ogata; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention that because that's how it was presented to me and the minister, my minister, mentioned the places that I was supposed to visit because they were critical because the information about Brcko was that it was horrible, about Zvornik, Vlasenica, Prijedor. So according to those instructions I started with Hadzici, Ilidza, Vlasenica, Brcko, and Prijedor. These were the locations that I was supposed to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this report is P1607. The report is P1607. I just wanted to ask you a few questions about that report. First of all, the first section refers to Vlasenica and discusses a camp in a place called Luke. I just want you to confirm as you did in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case that that was a reference to Susica camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Susica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you for the improved pronunciation. The answer is yes; correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, there's also item 4 a discussion about Prijedor, and as I understand it, the information contained there was obtained during a meeting involving a number of officials from Prijedor including Milomir Stakic, Dr. Kovacevic, Simo Drljaca, and Srdjo Srdic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, and Srdja Srdic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, with -- you also address Sanski Most in that report. And there you say the information that there is a camp in Sanski Most is not correct. In that area only four people were taken prisoner and transferred to the Manjaca camp during combat activities. Now, Mr. Avlijas, although on its face it would suggest that you were saying that only four people had ever been taken prisoner in Sanski Most, you clarified in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case that you were only talking about how many Muslim prisoners remained after the others, well over a thousand, had been transferred to Manjaca; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: At the time of my report they were all in Manjaca. I was interested in Sanski Most, but I was unable to get there because of the fighting. The information about the four men I received from the security officer, so it wasn't direct knowledge of mine. It was something that I learned indirectly, and I believe I said so in my Zupljanin-Stanisic testimony. So this wasn't direct first-hand information, but because I was supposed to go from Prijedor to Sanski Most and was unable to, so I contacted the responsible persons who were privy to the information and that's the information that I received from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. I think as you testified in Stanisic-Zupljanin, you -- at 15268, you spoke to a security officer from the Krajina Corps and then said: "There was no reason for me to disbelieve him," and "I had no time ..."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in this same report you refer to visits to Ilidza and Hadzici and I wanted to ask you some questions about those. The Hadzici section, which is found at the back of the report, item 10, states that 90 prisoners of war are accommodated in the Hadzici sports centre. Now, those 90 prisoners were people who had been taken prisoner back in May 1992 by the army, right? You testified to that at 15629 of the Stanisic-Zupljanin case.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, who else could have arrested them if not the army, military formations or the police? Well, some of those. Some -- I don't know who arrested them, but someone from the armed forces arrested them, and they were in Kula when they were arrested. Now, as for the group of 90 -- may I continue? Well, the group of 90 men that I found in the sports hall in Hadzici was a group that had been brought from Koviljaca in Ilidza municipality. That's on the border with Herceg-Bosna and Kiseljak where an exchange had fell through and they were there at night and they couldn't be returned to their original place. Now you can see -- you can look at the date. By that time, half of the men had already been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. Let me stop you because I wanted to move through it slightly more chronologically and get --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- to that point. Now, after having been taken prisoner in May 1992, they were first in the sports centre, then transferred to Kula where they stayed until September, October when this failed exchange that you just referred to took place; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And before their transfer to Kula, these people had been "viciously mistreated," those were your words, in Hadzici. As you put it in another part of your testimony in Stanisic-Zupljanin: "They had gone through horrific torture by paramilitaries in Hadzici."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I'm a man who lived for 17 years in Hadzici. When the Hadzici people were brought to Kula, to the camp, I had a moral obligation as a citizen, as a person living in that town, because there were a lot of friends among them, my son's best friend. So I had a moral obligation to visit those people, because they saw their chance when they heard that I was there. I know -- I asked the authorities, the guards who secured them, and we weren't the ones who did that. The police did. I asked them to let me get inside, and then I talked to those men and they told me about the difficulties and the problems they had with these people but not at the hands of the locals but from these members from various paramilitary groups that kept coming to Hadzici. So that was why I intervened. I intervened that those people be removed from Hadzici as soon as possible and so that they could be helped.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the last portion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may intervene in the transcript. There are several comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably, Mr. Avlijas, you are speaking too fast, way too fast. The interpreter did not get the last portion of your answer. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say anything after having said: "I intervened that those people be removed from Hadzici as soon as possible and so that they could be helped"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said this in the context of my earlier story. These were people I knew. I lived there, and I knew the difficulties they had and the things they suffered at the hands of the paramilitaries before they were moved to Kula. Now, this was a group of prisoners who had been returned to the same place from which they had been taken to Kula after two or three months because of this failed exchange, so I begged these people be removed from there for their own safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, in his answer on page 86, the word "arrested" is used repeatedly, but the witness did not say "arrested." He said "taken prisoner." And also on page 87, the witness said the people who suffered not at the hands of the locals and the army but at the hands of the paramilitaries. And one more thing, he said that he exchanged kisses and embraced those people who were detained there. So not at the hands of the local authorities or the army but at the hands of the paramilitaries. We can ask the witness to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you referred more that once to these people as friends, you talked about exchanging kisses and embraces with them, and you said the same thing in Stanisic-Zupljanin: "I had a lot of friends there who found themselves in this misfortunate situation." That's at 15631. Now, can -- can I assume based on the fact that you were friends with them, Mr. Avlijas, that these were not a group of Islamic fundamentalists or Muslim extremists?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I did not see them in that light. Either I did not -- that's not how I perceived them. How could I perceive them as a fundamentalist or extremist when they were friends that I had socialised with for years, for 30 years or so? They were true friends. These were -- these were friends that I had socialised with for many years and I helped them not as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name of the person that the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I could not see him in that light. The best part of my life is when I lived there and I will never forget the citizens of Hadzici. When my two parents died the entire town came to see them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name Nermin did not make it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I remember that name Nermin, Mr. Avlijas. He was somebody who --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Nermin and Alem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Am I correct that he was someone who was actually crying when -- when he met you and --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: We were both crying. We both cried when we met. And the most moving scene was when I found the best friend of my son's. Of course we cried. He said, "Uncle Slobo, can you help me?" And I said, "Well, son, this -- it's wartime and of course I will find a way to help you. You cannot expect me to take you by the hand and just take you out with all these extremists being present there." And I even had to help my own people on several occasions because the times were such. These paramilitaries, they were dangerous 24 hours a day. There wouldn't be any time when they would put away their rifle.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Extremists on all three sides. That's something that did not -- that was not recorded in the transcript. And I would really appreciate the witness to speak a bit slower because important things are omitted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again you were told that these were people who had been captured in areas where combat was taking place or something to that effect; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, you see, if you're referring to this group of people, there was fighting in the entire area of Hadzici municipality, both in the town itself and outside. These were attacking, the others were defending themselves, so there was shelling all the time and combat all the time. Now whether these people were in fact prisoners of war, military prisoners or not, I really can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And you didn't make any effort at the time to determine whether their confinement was illegal and whether they should be immediately released, notwithstanding the fact that they were crying and begging for help.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Look, I was just a simple man who came to do my job on the 28th of May. They came in mid-June. I -- I didn't have an office or anything. I did not belong to any political option. I was left without any work in 1992. I was a man who was in hiding until May because I was afraid, and I also had to hide my son.
