So I was not in any position nor did I have any function so that I could intervene and tell anyone to do anything. You know, at that time whoever said anything, they did not fare well. You needed to be very wise to keep your skin. I was just a lawyer and I was in charge of penal and correctional facilities. So at that time it was bizarre, the position that I was in. People tried to use my previous reputation when I was the president of the court and when I was a municipal legal officer, so that's how people saw me, what I was before the war. And knowing me and what kind of person I was, they thought that I could help them too, and as a human being I did my best to help them, not as a person who was in any possession in the judicial system to help them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last portion of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again your last part wasn't heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know there's anyway to retrieve it, Mr. President. We can play the tape back but I just fear if we ask again, we'll get a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we should --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- repetition of the entire answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We heard sufficient answer. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you a few questions, then, about Kula, Mr. Avlijas. Now your statement indicates that you were there. It's also correct that Mr. Mandic had an office there, right? And that's what you testified to in the Lalovic case. Sorry. I know you're nodding your head affirmatively, but if you can just say yes orally instead -- okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Kula was secured by the police, by the MUP; correct? You also testified to that in Lalovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, just a couple of questions about who was confined in Kula. You already mentioned the presence of people from Hadzici, and you clarified in the Mandic trial that it wasn't the entire population of Hadzici that was imprisoned at Kula, but "the group was fairly large group." And that's at Mandic, page 39; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition among the people who were in Kula during the time you were there were people who were "collected" from Dobrinja, from Grbavica, and those residents were taken to Kula. I think your quote was. "You know that after the attacks then, when they collected people from Dobrinja, from Grbavica, and these residents were taken to Kula." And that was at -- that's what you testified to in the Lalovic case, right, about some of the people who were present in Kula?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it again from your Lalovic testimony, for the most part you could not approach these people and speak to them about their situation, how they got there, how they were doing, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question. How the prisoners of war got there or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understood from your Lalovic testimony at English page 24 that you couldn't approach the prisoners and speak about their situation; right? That's what you testified to at that page.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you really didn't know about the conditions, for example, you didn't know how many meals per day the prisoners got.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Up until the 1st of August, 1992, the detained persons were guarded by the officials of the internal affairs which was proved in this case. We could only access them with the approval of the chief of the centre. And when I went the to visit the Hadzici people, I asked -- I appealed with the minister to allow me, to enable me to get in there. There was no other way I could get there. Now, as soon as you detain a person, it's not a pleasant condition, but the conditions were, relatively speaking, satisfactory. The food, I know that we had breakfast at 8.00, and then as we were leaving that cafeteria, they were coming in. So the food that we were served was the food they were served. It was the same. But we ourselves didn't have much food. We lived there off of a farm that was -- there was a pig farm and a chicken farm and some vegetables available there and that's what we used as food. Later on, the Red Cross came and they assisted us with foodstuffs. So there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one thing and I know in your statement you indicated that there was a sort of a common cauldron, but you were asked about that in the Mandic case too and you clarified there at page 29 that you simply were not in a position "because it wasn't my area of jurisdiction" to know how many meals per day, "two or three, believe me, I don't know, because it wasn't my area of" -- okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. I wasn't there. It wasn't part of my job and I couldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as we discussed with previous situations where you encountered persons being held, you assert that you could not say precisely what their status was, civilian or combatant. And in that regard, you were shown a document during the course of the Stanisic-Zupljanin case reflecting that 114 persons in Kula were moved to the Vrbanja Bridge area and sent into the city down Sokolovic Street, persons who had been in Kula since the 12th of May. And that's P1151. And in answering questions about that, first you -- about that particular document, first you explained the general geography of the area where the Vrbanja Bridge was, where Sokolovic Street was, and then you said: "There must have been an assessment to the effect that they no longer needed to be kept in custody throughout the war. All exchanges took place along separate lines, and the bridge on Vrbanja was a central location where forces, people moved from Republika Srpska into the federation and back. This is where civilians were usually released and exchanged." And that's at transcript 15581 through 82. Can you confirm that was your testimony in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, there is no reason not to confirm it. Perhaps I need to explain something. During the fighting in Dobrinja I, II, III, and IV, there were mass escapes. People fled to the -- to the KPD in order to find shelter there, but then there was a separation. The people were separated and taken, those 200 or so that you mentioned, they were taken to the Vrbanja Bridge, because even if someone wanted to keep them there, it would not be possible. These were just regular citizens. There were people, men, women, elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 37 of your statement, you discuss the Koricanske Stijene event, and you talk about a meeting you attended in Banja Luka where a discussion was held about what you describe as an incident that took place there, and you explain that the president of the Municipal Assembly Radic and the military insisted that perpetrators of the crime be arrested and processed. You indicate your recollection that the meeting determined that the crime was committed by a breakaway group of policemen on their own volition, and "Simo Drljaca informed us that these policemen were on the run." You recall an investigation was ongoing. Zupljanin said he had formed a team and a criminal report was filed, and that Drljaca said he tried to arrest the perpetrators but they were on the run and subject to a search warrant. And the statement goes on to talk about Trnopolje as part of a further discussion at that meeting. So I wanted to talk to you then about where this statement stops and what other information you've provided to this Court or other courts in other cases. First of all, let me identify the persons who were present at that meeting and you've previously testified that among the persons present beyond Mr. Radic were Milan Trbojevic, the vice minister of the government; Dragan Kalinic, the minister of health; and Bogdan Subotic, the minister of defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that Bogdan Subotic was there well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Stojan Zupljanin and Simo Drljaca were there, also Mr. Radic and also some basic and district prosecutors. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: The presidents of the county courts were there, then the municipal prosecutor, the representative of Banja Luka, and a person from the Banja Luka Corps. It was a meeting attended by the most senior persons from the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. The existence or the fact that this crime and the fact that it had been committed by members of the SJB Prijedor commanded by Simo Drljaca was no secret; right? And that's what you testified to in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case. Let's -- quote: "... let's not reinvent the wheel here. The entire RS knows that it was done by members of the SJB in Prijedor, commanded by Simo Drljaca."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Literally we say "hot water."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And that's at T15659. And then you said further about how well it was known. "It is no secret at all, and it was known on that day of the meeting. The entire Krajina and all of the RS knew that the police station, or SJB, I'm not sure of the exact name at the time, was in charge of escorting a civilian convoy, a convoy of civilian population, I think predominantly of Muslim ethnicity ..."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. In fact you said the only thing that wasn't known is whether it was active-duty officers or reserve police officers who had done it. There was no -- quote: "There was no doubt about whether or not the crime had been committed or not. Everything was known." Right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then you went on to say in Stanisic-Zupljanin, if it had been -- this is a quote. "... if it had been a well-functioning state, Simo Drljaca should have been locked up. If there is command responsibility in a well-functioning state, then there can be no discussion about it." Right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Yes, but I said one more thing that probably was not recorded. The chance of arresting Simo Drljaca at that point in time was very poor given the security situation in the RS. Simo Drljaca had built an image of a warlord in the Krajina at the time. So tactics what was required. But very soon after that, Simo Drljaca was no longer the chief of the Prijedor police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He was actually somebody who went to the exchange commission along with you and also an assistant minister of police, of the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I don't know if he was assistant minister. He may have been for a very short while until he was replaced, but he was a member of the exchange commission, one who never attended a meeting. And I think, but I cannot be fully sure, that he very soon left the RS and spent most of his time at Zlatibor. Anyway, that -- those were the stories that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the course of the Stanisic-Zupljanin case where you also made the point as you have -- as you did a moment ago about Mr. Drljaca as image of warlord or something to that effect in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case, you were confronted with the fact that Prijedor was in the vicinity of the 1st Krajina Corps and all of its troops. You were confronted with the fact that the MUP had very well armed, well trained and well equipped special units. And essentially you were confronted with the fact that it was certainly physically possible to arrest Mr. Drljaca had there been any will to do so; right? And what you said at that time was: "What I'm --" I'll just tell you what you said and you can expand on it if you want. "What I'm saying is had the state been functioning properly, he should have been arrested. Why wasn't he arrested? I don't know. I'm answering you in such a way ... what I would have done had I been in power, for instance." Can you confirm that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I confirm that I said that, and I've been trying all the time to say that from this distance in time, we cannot look upon the RS as a state who had come to high positions and who were nobodies before. They had no experience with running a state. A state, a real state, which executes all its remit, in such a state there is no doubt that Simo Drljaca would have been arrested immediately after the crime at Koricanske Stijene, because he tarnished the honour of the Serbian soldier and there can be no justification for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during the course of your testimony in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case, when asked about this very issue and describing something similar to what you're saying now, you said that the problem was -- or laid the problem at the doorstep of the SDS. So when you were talking about the difference in a well -- what would happen in a well-functioning state but what happened in this case, then you -- you added: "And I can say openly ... that I told the investigators when they asked me about staffing and dealing with personnel issues, it was the SDS that was consulted about everything, and I asked whether -- or, rather, I was asked whether a minister could appoint anyone, and I answered that he could when he got approval to do so." That's what you said in Stanisic-Zupljanin at page 15665; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you also said one page later, it had to be carefully considered what to do when replacing people, and: "... I believe it was the SDS's fault that they didn't allow the professionals to do their work." Correct? You stated that as well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Those are my thoughts. I may have been wrong, but it is my conviction that they remained fully professional, but unfortunately the RS at the outset didn't have any kind of organisation, but both Crisis Staffs and municipalities and everything else was built as we were going along. If professionals had been in positions of responsibility, such things would never have happened. Wherever there were professionals in such positions, in the federation with the Bosniaks or on our side, the likelihood of such things occurring would have been minimal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And perhaps last question, let me just check one thing very quickly, sir. And last question. Were you aware that on the 26th of November, 1993, Dr. Karadzic awarded the Petar Mrkonjic medal to the police station in Prijedor and the Karadjordjeva medal to the former head and now assistant in the Ministry of Interior, Simo Drljaca. Did you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I didn't. No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's P4261. And I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Avlijas, let us start with the last thing the Prosecutor dealt with. You speak about it in paragraph 37 also. And you mentioned that Drljaca, in your opinion, should have been held responsible on the basis of command responsibility. Did you learn about any information that he actively participated in that crime? Not only that the perpetrators were under his command, that he actually commanded the crime.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. At the meeting he said that it was a group of breakaway policemen who committed that crime. So there was no order to commit it. When the centre chief, Stojan Zupljanin, informed those present that he had filed criminal charges against unknown perpetrators -- and last time I said that it was a matter to -- a matter for Mr. Puaca, the district prosecutor for Banja Luka, to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, the witness said "breakaway police officer." Did you say "breakaway" or "regular"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Breakaway, renegade, because this term "breakaway" or "renegade" police officers was used all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that meeting, you stated that legal steps were taken. Did you know that anything had been done to cover up that crime?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No, at no point in time. All those present were -- were appalled, and they said that we won't let a group of criminals to tarnish the whole Krajina. It was very emotional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 98 of today's transcript, you said that -- it was not recorded that there was no functioning system in place. This was not recorded. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether the leaders of the RS favoured that situation for this -- the dysfunctionment of the system, and what was the attitude of both me and the Presidency in that respect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Based on a number of guidelines, orders, instructions, and other regulations, it can clearly be seen that the president and the government made efforts for the state to function in order with our rules and regulations. However, how that was implemented on the ground, I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were saying that state institutions were being built from scratch, do explain to the Trial Chamber what we were able to keep once Bosnia-Herzegovina had fallen apart and why we had to start from scratch.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, the whole infrastructure was in Sarajevo. We didn't even have desks or chairs, let alone rules and regulations and everything else. So we had to start by drafting laws, and everything we were able to keep was left intact. And then we went to Montenegro because they had the same rules and regulations as Bosnia-Herzegovina had had. And then we went law by law, regulation by regulation, and so on, and that's how we worked from the very outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please make a pause between question and answer, and do enunciate the way I do so that everything can be recorded. On page 95, you were asked about civilians who were -- who found refuge in the KPD. Were those civilians evicted to Sarajevo against their will?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. There was widespread horror at the beginning of the war. We didn't -- people didn't know where the border was, where the fighting was. People were fleeing in order to preserve their lives. If you cut off somebody's way of retreat, for example, the Muslims to flee to town, it is normal for people to escape to where some infrastructure was to save themselves. Many people were left behind and they wanted to join their families, and the place to meet the families was the Vrbanja Bridge. Many Serbs -- Serbs were leaving Sarajevo and the others were moving in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was said that those people were civilians from Dobrinja and Grbavica. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how far the war zone was from Dobrinja or Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: In Dobrinja there was a -- Dobrinja was in fact a war zone, and Grbavica was along the Miljacka River. So we're talking about streets, a distance measured in streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Concerning these departures upon request, were the Presidency or the government in a position to forbid that, and how would that have looked with regard to the rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, everybody would interpret it the way that suited them. We respected the will of the people to join their families, and I think it's normal for people to go where they feel safer. Once bullets fly around you, you want to be safe. Others saw that as ethnic cleansing. In such situations, it is very difficult to be realistic in assessing people's behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever establish that either the government or the Presidency or I personally supported ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: No. That cannot be found in any one document. And if -- nobody has ever ordered me anything of that kind, nor did my ministry deal with anything of the sort. I never heard in the news that somebody -- or that anybody ordered for some village to be cleansed or people to be evicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 81, the question was asked why you were sent to the field, wherever. After the first visits, the first audit, it was established that you were very strict. Is that why you were removed from your position or were you criticised from anybody from the government or from the Presidency or myself for being so strict?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was not interpreted well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Was he criticised by me, by anyone from the government, or the ministry for being strict, and was he removed from his position, or was he sent to conduct further audits?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I continued to do that work, and nobody ever had any objections to my reports. They were submitted to the minister, and I was -- but I was never criticised by the government. I was always very frank and very strict. On the contrary, my minister Jovo Rosic and Minister Kalinic insisted that I be appointed as a member of the commission in April 1993. In November 1993, the 3rd of November, I was appointed assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that a promotion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, probably somebody valued my work and thought that I was the one who could engage in the work of implementing criminal sanctions because I was a responsible person in my job. Although I must immediately add that I did not belong to any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's what I was going to ask you, but what was your question whether that was -- what is your answer to the question whether that was a promotion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. I was a coordinator, but in November 1993, I became assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you need a recommendation or the support of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: I didn't need any recommendation at the time. The only recommendation was my work and the minister's opinion that nobody was better suited for the job, and the government accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You began to speak about the ways information was received from foreigners and what happens to it later, and then there was talk of pressure. Tell us first whether the information received from international representatives and from the media, especially Muslim media, was true, whether they depicted the situation realistically, or whether they depicted it as being better or worse than in reality.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: We received some information about Vogosca but we immediately refused that. I think it was you, but I'm not sure, or the government gave precise instructions as to which towns should be visited and I went from one to the other, and there was information that there were still camps in Vlasenica, Zvornik and Trnopolje. This stress was on that. In Vlasenica I found nothing. I must be honest, however, and it's mentioned in the statement, too, that there was a collection centre, some facility, warehouse in Susica, and I was informed that everybody had been exchanged. In Zvornik, I told you what I found, and in Brcko there was no one prisoner. I was able to come by a list of everybody who was killed in Brcko. There were about 50 people. And I made a proposal to the government that an identification be carried out by an international mediator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice or did you learn that I reacted and demanded the government and the ministry to do something only due to this pressure, or did I also react to other information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It can be seen in the archives that -- or, rather, how many instructions you gave out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can tell from the archives that there is -- there were zillions of guidelines, instructions, orders, and other relevant documents showing that President Karadzic took interest in what was going on and that he also issued instructions as to how they -- how these prisoners should be treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that merely a reaction to pressure? And you were going to say it but then you were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When Karadzic is informed, what would he do afterwards with the information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the first part of the question surely seems to be inviting speculation, and the second part, I haven't seen a basis in this witness's testimony to think he's in a position to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll rephrase. The pressure occurred in August. Did you see any of my documents before this pressure in August about the need to comply with the law?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: It was the Official Gazette 992 reflecting your order, paragraph 3, saying exactly what steps must be taken in terms of POW treatment. And then Minister Subotic also said in one of his final provisions who was responsible for the treatment of prisoners, the exact list of commanders and all their subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you perhaps remember the exact date and month?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us about Planjina's tower? Where was it located physically in relation to the bunker?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: That may have been an oversight on our part but nobody asked. When I looked for that facility to put people up, I tried to keep it as far away as I could from the front line. That was something that needed taking into account because, as a matter of fact, they were practically near Zuca itself. Then I wanted something, a building, in the general direction of Semizovac, something that would be further removed from the front lines that would also be fit to hold a remand prison as well as the prisoners there. So we moved them some 10 or 12 kilometres deep, and at this point they ended up being at least 15 kilometres from the actual front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What about Mr. Vlaco, could he do anything without your intercession? Was he in charge of Semizovac, or was it that he had something available to him but it was his intention to not put them up some place better, as simple as that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: He acted of his own accord and he answered to the Crisis Staff. Therefore I can't say. He probably sought out and found a location for that first accommodation they were given. The rest was done as per instructions, and the Crisis Staff determined that that should be the building used for that purpose. They also asked me whether that was the condition imposed and to be complied with based on the UN conventions on the treatment of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell us if the overall Muslim population was placed on remand or imprisoned, and what was the basis for their detention?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: You can't imprison a whole group of people like that, a whole nation. The basis was some people took part in combat and some other people were assisting the BH Territorial Defence in some way. Money, equipment, that kind of thing. And there were some combatants who were actually taken prisoner but who were not at the front line. But they were members of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Page 66 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- about that visit to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- shall we continue tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need no more than five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I will ask for leave for just one, just very discrete area with two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 66 you were asked about the visit to Herzegovina. You said that you travelled via Niksic. We know where Niksic is but the Chamber doesn't. Could you please explain, why did you take that route and where is Niksic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: When you travel from Sarajevo to Trebinje the distance is about 120 kilometres. For me to reach Trebinje, the circumstances being what they were, I had to take the road from Sarajevo to Zvornik, from Zvornik on to Zlatibor, from Zlatibor to Pljevlja, and then on to Podgorica, and from Podgorica to Niksic. All in all about 1.000 kilometres as opposed to the original 120 in order to reach Bileca, so that was the differential.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Niksic, Podgorica, Zlatibor, where are all these places?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Niksic and Podgorica are in Montenegro, and Zlatibor is in Serbia. I had to cross two republics in order to reach my eventual destination, Bileca and Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question. You said that the prisoners of war were under the army's jurisdiction. Who had the authority to make decisions concerning civilian prisoners, and who had the power to make decisions about military prisoners? And were there any military judicial bodies at the time when you were on your way to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to see how -- I don't know where -- if this is a reference to the cross-examination, I can't recall a comment or question that was framed in that precise manner, so I just fear that Mr. Karadzic is carving out in his question some distinctions that he hopes to lead the witness to. But I don't -- unless he directs me to it, I don't take that as a fair assessment of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the issue arose during your cross whether certain power fell on the civilian authority including the witness or to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll say my recollection is that the witness said repeatedly he didn't know the status of those people and then -- but he did talk about who had ordered their confinement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you go back to pages 73 and 74, it wasn't just about taking prisoners. It's also about the fate of those people and who could change or influence the position that they were in. He said it wasn't him, it was the judiciary. That he said about the civilian prisoners. Now, I'm asking him about the POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What section of the army was in a position to affect their circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Perhaps you should explain the difference between people being on remand and being prisoners. So remand is one thing and we needn't go into that. That's for the civilian judiciary to deal with. It's the civilian courts that should be dealing with that and deciding on the fate of the persons on remand, awaiting trial. Prisoners are a totally different thing. This has nothing to do with the Law on Criminal Procedure. These persons were under the army's jurisdiction and nobody else's but theirs. For a while at Kula our only task was to make sure they were safe, keep them from being mistreated and to make sure they had enough food to eat. Any exchanges that were conducted and anything else, none of that could be done without the army's presence or assent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just my very last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about crimes under the military law? Under whose jurisdiction was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN AVLIJAS
utterances.text: Under the jurisdiction of the Military Court once it was constituted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Avlijas, for your testimony, and thank you very much for having been intransigent while carry out your tasks of state control back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This arises out of the question about strictness and even now comments about intransigence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Avlijas, can you confirm your evidence in the Lalovic case that you were aware in 1992 that persons confined in Kula were being taken away for the needs of the army but you didn't know, and I'll give you the quote: "I don't know what they were taken for the needs the army but I don't know what these needs of the army were, probably digging trenches and the rest. What else could they do? What else could they do for the army?" Can you confirm that was your testimony in Lalovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This could have been asked in -- covered in the cross-examination. I don't see where it really arises from the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that -- that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It could have been covered in but I tried to be as strict as possible, and now we've got a lot of emphasis on this witness's strictness and I'll follow it up with a last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you leave it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry -- well, I'd just like some confirmation of at least that part of the testimony since I asked the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But it opens up a whole other area of forced labour, Mr. President, that I don't think would be correct given the limited nature of what he's trying to accomplish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the time. Let's leave it there, Mr. Tieger. Thank you, Mr. Avlijas. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of March, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.55 p.m.,
